comments.body:
🤖 Final results: SFT vs rejection-sampled SFT vs on-policy distillation for transferring the CruxEval expert back into B

TL;DR. All three arms recover most or all of the expert's CruxEval gain. Every arm trains on prompts drawn from the same 1,600 the evaluator scores (800 input-prediction and 800 output-prediction problems; plain SFT and OPD use all 1,600, RS-SFT the 1,503 with an execution-correct E sample), so this is transfer on seen prompts. Two-pass means on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0 (400 updates), RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9 (283 updates), OPD 79.6 / 75.2 (75 updates); the expert E scores 79.4 / 71.4 and B scores 55.4 / 57.8 (CruxEval input / output, pass@1 on 800 problems each). RS-SFT's two-pass means are 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD's; two passes on one run per arm do not resolve that ordering. Both are above plain SFT by 5.7–6.9 pp on input and 3.2–5.9 pp on output. Training cost: OPD 287 H100-h from allocation to the selected checkpoint (376 for the full 4-epoch run); plain SFT 62 and RS-SFT 57 for their full 4-epoch runs (the RS candidate is update 283 of 376 and was not timed separately). RS-SFT also used ground-truth execution results to pick its demos, which the other arms did not have. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K (B 90.4) or MATH500 (B 89.8); OPD 75 scores 90.4 on MATH500, 1.8 below E, inside MATH500's binomial 95% half-width of about 2.6 pp at n=500. These numbers do not measure generalization to unseen prompts.

Setup (the design doc is linked from the issue body).

- Student B: [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab).
- Expert E: B after full SFT on 1,454 [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, step 272 (35.9 H100-h); export [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). E+ (E + 2 epochs at 1e-6, 80.2 / 75.1) is a reference only.
- Evaluator: Evalchemy [ae362881](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8) (corrected 2026-10-13: the revision that actually ran is `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`, recorded in every record's `eval_runtime` field; `c131e5ab` was the code constant in `eval_policy.py`, which the launcher did not use. The scorer and sampling settings are the ones at ae362881 throughout, so no number changes.), vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking enabled, unseeded sampling at vLLM's default temperature 1.0 (the lm-eval chat client sends no sampling parameters). One pass has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp at n=800 (p≈0.55) and 3.0 pp at p≈0.75. Paired deltas use a problem-resampling bootstrap conditional on the sampled completions. Gist of all evaluator configs: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71.
- Matched AdamW hyperparameters across arms, in different implementations (Levanter for the SFT arms, Megatron for OPD): LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen (E froze it too; all exports verified to carry B's 26 router-bias tensors).
- Plain SFT: B + 4 epochs on E's first sample per prompt (1,600 rows, unfiltered), batch 16, 32 H100. 1,452,363 supervised tokens per epoch.
- RS-SFT: all 12,800 E samples (k=8) execution-graded in an isolated container; first correct sample per prompt kept. 1,503 of 1,600 prompts covered (774 input / 729 output); the 97 uncovered prompts stay in the eval denominator. 4 epochs, 376 updates. 1,056,479 supervised tokens per epoch.
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, B samples 4 rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E scores them (sampled reverse KL on the chosen tokens, coefficient 1.0, reward replaced by the distillation signal, no verifier). 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch, 4 epochs. 4 learner nodes (PP2 × EP8) + 1 rollout node + 1 teacher node, all H100x8.
- Selection procedure used (the rule 'prefer the final checkpoint when similar or better on both directions' was agreed before the final checkpoints were scored; the operational reading of similar as 'paired 95% CI includes 0' was fixed while applying it): if the final checkpoint is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions on the first pass, select it; otherwise run a second pass on both checkpoints and choose on the two-pass means. GSM8K and MATH500 run on the selected checkpoint and on any terminal checkpoint that lost the selection.

Results. CruxEval pass@1 (%), input / output. "Gap closed" is the gain over B divided by E's two-pass gain over B (24.06 pp input, 13.63 pp output). GSM8K (flexible-extract, 0-shot) and MATH500 are single pass for every model.

| Model | Input | Output | Gap closed | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 |
| E (CruxEval 2-pass mean) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT, 400 updates (2-pass mean) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 |
| RS-SFT, 283 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 |
| OPD, 75 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 |

Learning curves (single pass per checkpoint; the training trajectory, not the selection basis):

| Arm | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 | Epoch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain SFT (101/201/301/400 updates) | 69.6 / 67.5 | 73.5 / 69.9 | 69.4 / 71.8 | 74.8 / 71.3 |
| RS-SFT (95/189/283/376 updates) | 75.5 / 72.0 | 82.0 / 75.8 | 81.4 / 77.1 | 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD (25/50/75/100 updates) | 74.9 / 68.9 | 81.8 / 75.8 | 79.0 / 76.8 | 80.9 / 72.3 |

Selection. Plain SFT's final checkpoint was similar or better than its epoch-3 checkpoint on both directions (+5.4 / −0.5 pp), so it was selected and repeated (second pass 73.1 / 72.8). RS-SFT's final checkpoint was 4.4 pp below epoch 3 on input, and OPD's final checkpoint was 4.5 pp below epoch 3 on output, each with a paired CI excluding 0. Both arms got a second pass on their last two checkpoints. RS-SFT: 376 updates 76.1 / 76.2 against 283 updates 80.8 / 77.9 (two-pass means); the final is lower on both directions, so 283 was selected. OPD: 100 updates 79.875 / 72.0 against 75 updates 79.625 / 75.19; input differs by 0.25 pp and the final is 3.19 pp lower on output, so 75 was selected. The terminal checkpoints are reported in the curve table, not as the method result. The second passes reuse the same runs, so the four pass pairings per arm are one comparison, not four. Same-checkpoint pass pairs moved by up to 3.1 pp (OPD 75 output: 76.75 on pass 1, 73.6 on pass 2, paired CI [−6.0, −0.25]), so the conditional problem-bootstrap intervals do not capture all generation variability; two repeats are too few to estimate it. The final-checkpoint drops are therefore suggestive, not established.

Paired comparisons at the selected checkpoints (pass 1 vs pass 1; 95% bootstrap CI): RS-SFT 283 vs OPD 75: +2.4 [−1.0, +5.8] input / +0.4 [−2.5, +3.3] output on pass 1, and 0.0 [−3.4, +3.3] / +5.0 [+2.0, +8.0] on pass 2. RS-SFT 283 vs plain 400: +6.6 [+3.1, +10.1] / +5.9 [+2.8, +9.3] (pass 2: +7.1 / +5.9). OPD 75 vs plain 400: +4.3 [+0.9, +7.9] / +5.5 [+2.3, +8.8] (pass 2: +7.1 / +0.9 [−2.3, +4.0]). Against E (pass 1): RS-SFT 283 +2.0 [−1.5, +5.5] / +6.9 [+3.8, +10.1]; OPD 75 −0.4 [−3.8, +3.0] / +6.5 [+3.5, +9.5]; plain 400 −4.6 [−8.4, −1.0] / +1.0 [−2.4, +4.5]. Pass-1 and pass-2 pairings share the training runs; they are two draws of the evaluator, not two experiments.

Response shape: B leaves no final answer after the thinking block in 1,110 of 1,600 CruxEval responses; E in about 90. The same count was not made for the three arms, so part of each arm's gain may be this shape change. The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model. Correct/n on pass 1 and pass 2: B 1/26, 1/71; E 2/26, 1/71 and 1/26, 4/71; plain 400 0/26, 3/71 and 0/26, 4/71; RS-SFT 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71; OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71. The slice was selected by E failing all 8 samples on these prompts, so E's low score is selection-induced. RS-SFT saw no demos for these prompts. Comparing different methods on 97 selected prompts does not identify the effect of omitting them, so these are counts only.

Cost (H100-hours, Iris task-runtime accounting). Training figures are full-run costs for 4 epochs and include in-gang startup, native saves and exports; they exclude CPU preprocessing, demo generation and evals. The selected RS-SFT checkpoint is update 283 of 376 and the selected OPD checkpoint is update 75 of 100; costs are not pro-rated to the candidate. OPD's allocation-to-checkpoint figure comes from the run's log timestamps and ends at the checkpoint request, so it excludes the native save; plain SFT's 61.6 runs through its final HF export and job teardown. The two selected-cost endpoints are therefore not identical.

| Arm | Training (full 4-epoch run) | Demo generation | Exports | Allocation to selected checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E (expert) | 35.9 for 3 epochs (+15.3 in aborted attempts) | GLM traces via relay, no GPU-h on our side | in-gang | — |
| Plain SFT | 61.6 | shares the one k=8 E collection (14.6 measured once for all 12,800 demos, plus a 0.7 pilot; plain used 1 of the 8 samples, and no standalone 1-sample generation run was timed) | in-gang | 61.6 (final checkpoint selected) |
| RS-SFT | 57.4 | the same k=8 E collection (14.6, counted once for both SFT arms) + CPU execution grading | in-gang | full run 57.4; update 283 was not timed separately |
| OPD | 376.4 (6 nodes × 7h50m) | none (on-policy) | 58.8 (4 export-only jobs, 14–15 each) | 286.9 from allocation start to the update-75 checkpoint request (before the native save completes), plus its 14.2 export job |

OPD also spent 73.5 H100-h on smoke tests, debugging and the export path and 4.6 on a startup failure (missing W&B key) before the full run. These training-only figures are not the experiment total; the ledger adds evaluation (about 3.3 per CruxEval pass), failed-eval overhead, E and E+ training, and the reference runs. OPD per-update wall time was 4–5 min (256 sampled responses, 30,720-token cap) against about 17 s per SFT update; one prompt epoch is 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD and 1 demo for SFT, so epochs are matched on prompts, not on tokens or compute. One CruxEval pass costs about 3.3 H100-h; the ledger lists every eval run. Failed eval groups (serve preemption with a stale endpoint in the eval runner, and one preflight disconnect; see below) cost about 11 H100-h.

Confidence. The gains over B are large relative to noise (the lower 95% bound of every arm's paired gain over B is at least 9.8 pp). Between arms, the measured two-pass means put RS-SFT 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD and both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; each arm is one training run with no LR sweep, same-checkpoint pass pairs moved 0.5–3.1 pp on the six repeated checkpoints, and two repeats do not estimate run-to-run variance, so the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering is unresolved and the gap to plain SFT is the better-supported difference. The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

Artifacts. The full results ledger (every record id, paired comparison and cost): https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0 (also in the collapsed section at the end of this comment). Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces with a side-by-side compare view): https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/<record>/record.json`. OPD W&B: marin-community/skyrl run p3ie2bg7. Training jobs: `/karan/task145-plain-sft-20261008`, `/karan/task145-rs-sft-20261009`, `/karan/opd-crux-e-full-launch-2`. Selected HF exports: plain [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399 @ 3e34be3f](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399/tree/3e34be3f884ff737f85354b060ea831ce0c90636) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`), RS-SFT [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282 @ 073d128c](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282/tree/073d128cb1e53652126cce37a7cc2c96625d3c80) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`), OPD [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75 @ 9d189320](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75/tree/9d1893207226cf72f701187e1d5260d9fc3c931d) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`), E [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). Other epochs sit beside them (`step-100/200/300`, `step-94/188/375`, `global_step_25/50/100`).

Next. Weight merging is out of scope here (it needs RL-trained experts that share B's initialization). Open questions this run cannot answer: whether the ordering holds on held-out prompts, whether an LR sweep changes it, and whether OPD's per-update cost can be cut with fewer rollouts or a shorter generation cap.

## Caveats

Test-exposed prompts (all arms train on the eval set); RS-SFT uses ground-truth execution correctness to filter demos (verifier access that plain SFT and reward-replace OPD do not have) plus 8 teacher samples per prompt; supervised-token budgets differ across arms; gains include response-shape change (B leaves no

batch/update geometry (16 rows/update vs 64 prompts × 4 rollouts), optimizer implementation (Levanter vs

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval SFT, LR 1e-5, 3 ep) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT step 399 | 0.123 | 0.30 | 0.27 | 0.31 | 0.022 | 0.41 | 41.2 | 0.05 | 0.08 | 0.05 | 0.68 |
| RS-SFT step 282 | 0.094 | 0.24 | 0.21 | 0.25 | 0.015 | 0.34 | 34.5 | 0.06 | 0.09 | 0.07 | 0.71 |
| OPD update 75 | 0.035 | 0.12 | 0.077 | 0.12 | 0.006 | 0.060 | 20.3 | 0.08 | 0.12 | 0.12 | −0.32 |

Reading:
- Everything is a small perturbation: no checkpoint moves more than 0.13% of B's weight norm overall, and the largest component change is the expert's attention at 0.65%.
- The expert (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 1,454 rows) concentrates its change in attention, the router and the LM head and leaves the MoE expert MLPs almost untouched (0.047%, 13% of weights changed). The two SFT transfer arms (LR 1e-6, 4 epochs, 1,500–1,600 rows of the expert's text) do the opposite: they move the expert MLPs 4–6× more than the expert did and touch 35–41% of all weights. OPD moves least of the three arms (0.035% overall, comparable to the expert) and touches 20%.
- Direction: none of the arms re-creates the expert's weight change. The cosines between an arm's delta and E's delta are 0.05–0.12 in attention and the expert MLPs (random directions in this dimension give ≈0). The one shared direction is the LM head, where plain SFT and RS-SFT align with E (cosine 0.68 and 0.71) while OPD moves the LM head the opposite way (−0.32). Recovering the expert's CruxEval score therefore does not require copying its weights; three different weight changes produce it.
- RS-SFT changes the weights less than plain SFT (0.094% vs 0.123% overall) while scoring higher; it trains on fewer, verifier-correct rows.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights. Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Weight-delta direction for this experiment: does the OPD update point the same way as the expert update? Same method as the #9984 follow-up.

## Method

Deltas against the student B (`Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ fdc3c3c5) for expert E (step 272) and the three selected checkpoints: OPD update 75, plain SFT step 399, RS-SFT step 282. Per component: the Frobenius norm of each delta (absolute and relative to B), cosine with E's delta, sign agreement on weights changed in both, and subspace overlap. Overlap is the share of a delta's energy inside E's top-k singular directions per matrix, with k holding 50% of E's energy, compared with a random k-dim subspace and with E's delta permuted within each matrix. E's norms reproduce the earlier weight-delta table exactly. Script: `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_subspace.py` on branch `task/239` (711ba609ae).

## Result

All weights, against E:

| Delta | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ | weights changed | cos vs E | sign agree | overlap (random) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E | 0.0366% | 13.7% | — | — | — |
| OPD update 75 | 0.0355% | 20.3% | 0.079 | 0.598 | 0.203 (0.101) |
| RS-SFT step 282 | 0.0938% | 34.5% | 0.058 | 0.581 | 0.196 (0.108) |
| Plain SFT step 399 | 0.1236% | 41.2% | 0.045 | 0.562 | 0.184 (0.108) |

Overlap with E's half-energy subspace, as a multiple of the random null:

| Component | OPD 75 | RS-SFT 282 | plain SFT 399 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attention | 3.9× | 3.0× | 2.7× |
| Expert MLPs | 1.9× | 1.7× | 1.6× |
| Shared experts | 4.0× | 2.6× | 2.2× |
| Router | 3.7× | 2.2× | 2.1× |
| LM head | 391× | 710× | 686× |

## Reading

- **Same pattern as #9984, and stronger.** OPD shares direction with E more than either SFT arm in attention, expert MLPs, shared experts and over all weights. It is also more aligned than the MOPD update was there (all-weights cosine 0.079 vs 0.049).
- **Size.** OPD moves the weights about as much as E did (0.036% of ‖B‖). The SFT arms move them 2.6–3.4× more, mostly in the expert MLPs (0.20–0.27% vs E's 0.05%).
- **Router.** OPD leaves the router almost untouched (0.006% of its norm, against E's 0.17%). Its router cosine with E equals the SFT arms' (0.15 vs 0.14–0.15); only its sign agreement and overlap are higher.
- **LM head.** The SFT arms align strongly with E (cosine 0.68–0.71). OPD moves inside the same few top directions but with the opposite sign (cosine −0.32, sign agreement 0.26). MOPD showed the same flip in #9984 (−0.14), so it repeats across both experiments.
- **Small shared part.** 0.6% of OPD's update energy lies along E's delta, and 20% sits inside E's half-energy subspace against 10% at random. The transfer is mostly a different weight change that reaches the same behaviour.

## Limits

Correlational geometry only, with no ablation, so no causal claim about the scores. OPD 75 is the selected mid-run checkpoint, not the final update 100. The SFT arms train on E's own samples in one domain, which raises their alignment with E. bf16 exports hide changes below half an ulp, so every measure covers only what survived rounding.

| Arm, checkpoint (updates) | H100-h | trained tokens | input / output |
|---|---|---|---|
| B (start) | 0 | 0 | 55.4 / 57.75 |
| Plain SFT 101 / 201 / 301 / 400 | 30.2 / 45.6 / 61.0 / 76.2 | 1.5 / 2.9 / 4.4 / 5.8M | 69.6 / 67.5; 73.5 / 69.9; 69.4 / 71.75; 74.75 / 71.25 |

| E (expert, reference) | 35.9 | 1.8M | 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean) |

How the numbers are built:
- **H100-hours.** Each arm's measured training-gang allocation, pro-rated by updates.
- **SFT arms.** Each carries the 14.6 H100-h of the E demo collection from step 0.
- **OPD.** Each checkpoint carries its own export job, about 15 H100-h. Measured allocation-to-checkpoint for OPD, as a cross-check: 118.8 / 197.8 / 286.9 / 375.7 H100-h.
- **Trained tokens.** Loss-bearing tokens, counted each time they are trained on: SFT from the row manifests × epochs, OPD from the run's per-update scored tokens.
- **Excluded.** Evaluations, building E, and failed attempts.

Reading:
- **Cost to reach E's level.** RS-SFT passes E on both directions at update 189 (43.5 H100-h). OPD gets there at update 50 (203.3 H100-h), about 4.7× more GPU time.
- **Matched GPU-hours.** Both SFT runs ended (72 and 76 H100-h) before OPD's first checkpoint (108.5). At the SFT arms' final cost, a straight line from B to OPD update 25 puts OPD at about 68–69 / 65. That is an interpolation between two measured points, not a measurement.
- **Trained tokens.** OPD trains on 4–6× more tokens than the SFT arms, because it trains on its own, longer samples.

Caveats:
- This is not a matched-compute experiment: different optimizers, batch geometry and verifier access (RS uses execution correctness).
- Single passes unless marked; one pass is about ±3.5 pp.
- OPD's W&B history logged 99 of its 100 updates, so the final token count misses one update.

Full record, every evaluation id and the cost ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984#issuecomment-6144923850. **Eval policy results (updated 2026-11-06):** the full benchmark tables for this experiment's candidates are in [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984#issuecomment-6665513430) and are updated in place after each reviewed delta. ## Setup - **Student B**: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab). - **Expert E** (CruxEval, from #9920): [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). - **Expert E₂** (MMLU-Pro): B fine-tuned with E's recipe (full SFT, AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, frozen router bias, 32 H100, 60.6 H100-h) on 1,359 correct [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) traces over a seeded subset of 1,606 MMLU-Pro test questions; the other 10,426 questions were never trained on and serve as a probe. Browse the GLM, E and E₂ traces side by side: https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/ (public). [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254 @ acb97183](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254/tree/acb97183af633533df4f4f63d83adc1e0a7a9748) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task157-e2/checkpoints/karan/e2-mmlupro-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.09.1/hf/step-254`). - **Evaluator** (frozen, same as #9920): Evalchemy [ae362881](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8), vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking on, unseeded sampling at temperature 1.0. MOPD higher on CruxEval input, +4.9 [+1.6, +8.1]; CruxEval output unresolved, RS − MOPD +0.9 [−2.1, +3.75]. - **Against the experts**: both finals are above E on CruxEval output (MOPD +6.1 [+2.9, +9.4], RS +7.0 [+3.75, +10.4]) with input differences unresolved; on the MMLU-Pro subset MOPD − E₂ = −2.2 [−4.5, +0.1] and RS − E₂ = +1.7 [−0.5, +4.2]. Intervals that include 0 do not establish equivalence. - **Plain mixed SFT** is below RS-SFT by 5.8 [3.5, 8.2] on the MMLU-Pro subset and below E on CruxEval input. - **Merging** at half strength beats B in both domains with no training but stays 8–10 pp below the trained arms on CruxEval output; at full strength it regresses badly on GSM8K and GPQA-D with runaway generations. - **Collapse checks**: GSM8K at or above B for every trained arm; MATH500 and GPQA-D at or above B on the RS-SFT and MOPD finals (RS-SFT's GPQA-D 57.6 is +15.7 [+10.4, +21.0] over B, one evaluation, reported without interpretation); IFEval 1–3 pp below B (RS −2.8 [−5.2, −0.2], MOPD −1.1 [−3.6, +1.2]). ## Reading Two experts can be moved into B at once: both RS-SFT and MOPD improve both domains over B and land at or above each expert in that expert's domain on the point estimates. The two methods trade off by domain and are not matched controls for each other (RS-SFT had verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and a different token budget; MOPD cost 6× more H100-hours). Plain SFT recovers less; merging is a cheap partial substitute at half strength only. ## Caveats - One evaluation pass per checkpoint except the stated repeats; plain SFT's 803-vs-603 selection used two passes each. Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons or checkpoint selection. - Both primary targets are test-exposed (training-is-test); the held-out MMLU-Pro questions are an additional probe, never a selection input. - The RS-SFT demo selector used an older answer-extraction rule than the evaluator: 14 of its 1,400 MMLU-Pro demos are wrong under the evaluator's rule, 15 prompts would have been gained and 1 lost, 45 would have used a different sample. # Proposed Fix

1. After approval, train E₂ on the pinned canonical subset with E's #9920 recipe. Export it, evaluate B/E/E₂ on both target domains and the collapse checks, and apply the stated MMLU-Pro paired-gain and GSM8K gates. Stop the transfer arms if E₂ fails.
2. If E₂ passes, pin its k=8 demo collection and construct the two mixed SFT datasets from the same 3,206 prompts. Record rejection-sampling coverage and supervised token counts. Smoke the domain-routed MOPD setup, including teacher score alignment, one update, and HF export, before the four-epoch run.
3. Run MOPD, mixed SFT, and mixed SFT-RS from B with the issue's fixed optimizer and epoch budget. Use #9974 for the B/E/E₂ coefficient sweep and TIES/DARE-TIES after its tools are ready; verify checkpoint tensor alignment and complete exports.
4. Score each selected arm on CruxEval, MMLU-Pro (full set, training subset, held-out groups), GSM8K, GPQA-D, and MATH500 with the frozen evaluator. Report paired intervals, the issue's checkpoint-selection rule, verifier access for SFT-RS, and H100-hours in one final issue update. The trained MMLU-Pro and CruxEval prompts must be labeled as seen-prompt results.

🤖 **Final report: two experts into one student (MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merging)**

## Summary

E_2 reached 66.4% on the MMLU-Pro subset used for its fine-tuning (B 44.5%) and 64.0% on the remaining docs (B 44.1%). Its CruxEval output score was 4.9 percentage points below B in one pass. Its IFEval instruction-strict point estimate was also below B (80.2% versus 81.1%), with an interval spanning zero; the other reported probe point estimates were above B. At the selected finals, mixed SFT-RS step-727 exceeds MOPD step-100 on the MMLU-Pro subset by 4.0 pp [1.6, 6.3]; the held-out difference is unresolved (+0.4 [−0.5, 1.4]). MOPD exceeds RS on CruxEval input by 4.9 pp [1.6, 8.1]; the output difference is unresolved. MOPD = MarinSkyRL on-policy distillation with two pinned teachers, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (sampled reverse KL, 4 rollouts per prompt, 1:1 route mix). Mixed SFT = one demo per prompt (E's and E_2's sample 0 from k=8 pools). Mixed SFT-RS = the first sample per prompt in index order that is execution-correct (CruxEval) or accepted by the implemented answer selector (MMLU-Pro) from the same k=8 pools (1,503 + 1,400 covered prompts; uncovered prompts stay in every denominator). MMLU-Pro runs score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record's active FineStore snapshot against the canonical gold; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro (subset 1,589, held-out 10,212) and problems within each CruxEval direction (800), conditional on the observed sampled completions; they do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability. At ae362881, MMLU-Pro extraction uses final content when available, falls back to reasoning for REASONING_ONLY responses, and returns no answer for truncated reasoning-only responses; it applies `final_response_text`, then the three answer-letter regexes, and uppercases the result. Exact replay reproduced native predictions on all 12,032 rows of each of B-220c, E_2-254, RS-727 and MOPD-100. The broader matrix has uniform runtime-revision metadata; it was not replayed in full. The stored normalized output is not always the scorer input (the scorer saw the parser-split final content), so re-grading must start from the native completions. All comparisons are paired on the same docs.

## Reading the result

(1) At RS-727 and MOPD-100, both domains improve over B. Relative to the specialists, MOPD's MMLU-Pro subset difference from E_2 is −2.24 pp [−4.47, +0.06], while RS's is +1.74 pp with an interval spanning zero. Intervals spanning zero do not establish preservation or equivalence. Both checkpoints have higher CruxEval output scores than E's first pass; their input differences from E are unresolved. Paired changes versus B on each split: MOPD-100 +19.7 pp on the subset and +20.3 on the held-out docs; RS-727 +23.7 and +20.7. (2) RS-SFT and MOPD differ by domain: RS higher on the MMLU-Pro subset, MOPD higher on CruxEval input, output unresolved. RS-SFT had ground-truth verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and an unequal token budget; MOPD had on-policy samples scored by the teachers. Neither is a matched control for the other. (3) Plain mixed SFT recovers less than either (MMLU-Pro −5.8 pp vs RS; CruxEval below E on input). (4) Merging recovers CruxEval input (76.5 at a = b = 0.5) and most of MMLU-Pro (63.2) with no training, but its CruxEval output (67.6) is 2.6 pp below E's first pass (70.25), 3.8 below E's two-pass mean (71.4), 8.8 below MOPD-100 (76.4), 9.65 below RS-727 (77.25) and 3.9 below plain-803's first pass (71.5); TIES output (68.1) sits 0.5 pp above TA-0.5 on each of those comparisons; at full strength (a = b = 1.0) the merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs (median 85–95k characters), so it was withheld from the rest of the matrix. (5) Probes on the two finals (single pass each; 0 infrastructure-error rows; MATH500 median output 2,496 and 1,525 characters): RS-727 MATH500 92.4, GPQA-D 57.6, IFEval instruction-strict 78.3 (below B with the interval excluding 0: −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24]; loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 MATH500 90.0, GPQA-D 47.5, IFEval 80.0 (−1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] vs B). RS-727's GPQA-D score is above every other model in this matrix (B 41.9, E 44.8, E_2 47.6, MOPD-100 47.5, merges 47.1–47.3); it is one evaluation with three generations for each of 198 questions and is reported with its paired interval, not interpreted.

## Caveats

One pass per checkpoint except the explicitly reported repeats; plain 603/803 selection uses per-item two-pass means. Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons and checkpoint selection; additional-probe findings are exploratory. Targets are 800 problems per CruxEval direction and 1,606 docs; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro and problems within each CruxEval direction, conditional on the observed sampled completions, and do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability (E's two CruxEval passes differed by 0.1 / 2.25 pp in #9920). The MMLU-Pro subset was the fine-tuning set for E_2 and the training prompt set for every arm; the 10,426 held-out docs are an additional probe, reported and never used for selection. RS demo selector mismatch: the k=8 demo grader implemented the older first-match-anywhere extractor on the whole text, while the evaluator grades the final answer after the think block; under the evaluator's rule 14 of the 1,400 selected RS MMLU-Pro demos (1.0%) are wrong, 15 more prompts would have been covered and 1 lost, and 45 prompts would have used a different sample. The RS arm is reported as trained; no corrected run was made. Record provenance: two records (B MMLU-Pro and MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro) had a retried eval attempt that left a second full sample stream; all numbers here come from each record's pinned active FineStore manifest (HEAD), with the native writer taken from the active source-blob provenance (normalized sample rows can carry null correctness); superseded attempts are kept as overhead and evidence, not as independent repeats (an earlier reading of the first stream gave B 43.90 and MOPD-100 65.32 on the subset and has been superseded). Three merge MATH500 records from 2026-10-10 are invalid (Evalchemy `AgentTimeoutError` in 500/500, 455/500 and 300/500 rows) and were rerun for TA-0.5 and TIES; TA-1.0 was not rerun.

**Costs (H100-hours = GPUs × Iris task or attempt duration; method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298; every figure labelled by what it includes).** Training-gang allocations (image pull, load, steps, in-gang checkpoint/HF export and teardown; queue time excluded): E_2 60.6 (3 epochs, 32 H100). Mixed SFT-RS 93.57 (728 updates, 32 H100). Mixed SFT 107.83, plus 14.21 for a first attempt evicted by Kueue after 16 updates and relaunched from B. MOPD 557.9 for the 2-epoch run (100 optimizer updates, 7 × H100x8; the launch plan said ≈102, the sampler yielded 50 full windows per epoch; the W&B run `skyrl/snowball-mopd2-cruxeval-mmlupro-2ep` logged 99 steps and is marked `crashed`; coordinator logs record 100 updates and the terminal export at global_step 100 succeeded), plus 28.3 in two separate export-only jobs (step-50 13.8, step-100 14.5), which the SFT figures include in-gang; allocation to the step-50 checkpoint ≈ 317 and to step-100 ≈ 531 from timestamps (full run, not pro-rated). E_2 k=8 demo pool 8.91 (counted once, shared by both SFT arms; #9920's CruxEval pool is reused and its cost stays in #9920). Merges: CPU only (33, 28 and 68 min). Excluded from every total: GLM trace generation, E's construction (#9920), CPU preparation and audit jobs, the MOPD smoke run (≈60.6, reported in the design ledger). Evaluation serve allocation (serve attempt `started_at`→`finished_at` × 8 H100; queue time and CPU eval tasks excluded; two sweeps, 2026-10-13 05:20 and 11:40 UTC, 82 groups): 1,752.6 H100-h. Of this, 858.2 belongs to 51 groups with at least one successful eval child, including groups with invalid or superseded records; 894.5 belongs to 31 groups with no successful eval child. Per evaluated model (record / no-record): B 121.7 / 0; E 46.2 / 0; E_2 167.5 / 284.9; mixed plain 111.7 / 0; mixed RS 73.3 / 13.6; MOPD 112.0 / 0 (the step-50 retry alone 72.4: its MMLU-Pro eval ran 8 h 41 min without errors); merge TA-0.5 94.4 / 231.6; merge TA-1.0 79.9 / 241.6; merge TIES 51.6 / 122.7. Eight serves ran 13.8–14.6 h (110–117 H100-h each): six in the no-record bucket (`20261010-043736` E_2-85 MMLU-Pro, `20261010-030122` and `…030230` TA-1.0, `20261010-042000` and `…042104` TA-0.5, `20261010-042136` TIES; 689.4 together) and two in the record bucket (B's MMLU-Pro group `20261007-172014-…-9225`, 116.9, whose MMLU-Pro eval ran two attempts while its GPQA-D eval failed; E_2-85's `20261010-003548`, 110.3). Several of these groups have documented stale-endpoint failures after a serve preemption (#10030; its fix #10033 was not applied to this frozen evaluator), and B's group is documented as an eval retry after `PodDeleted`; the totals include all serve allocation regardless of cause, and the per-group attribution is only as complete as the overhead ledger's entries. These are infrastructure allocation costs, not inference-compute estimates. For scale, the #9984 training-gang allocations listed above sum to 834.1 H100-h (E_2 60.6 + RS 93.57 + plain 122.04 + MOPD 557.9), plus 28.3 of MOPD export-only jobs and 8.91 for the demo pool.

comments.body:
🤖

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages; cosines are given against E and against E₂.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro) | 0.035 | 0.64 | 0.043 | 0.067 | 0.15 | 0.11 | 12.9 | 0.21 vs E | 0.37 | 0.06 | 0.38 |
| Mixed plain SFT step 803 | 0.180 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.42 | 0.033 | 0.53 | 56.3 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.40 / 0.50 |
| Mixed RS-SFT step 727 | 0.171 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.40 | 0.030 | 0.49 | 54.7 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.42 / 0.51 |
| MOPD update 100 | 0.045 | 0.13 | 0.099 | 0.12 | 0.008 | 0.084 | 25.2 | 0.05 / 0.05 | 0.11 / 0.13 | 0.07 / 0.07 | −0.14 / −0.15 |
| Merge TA a = b = 0.5 | 0.031 | 0.53 | 0.041 | 0.064 | 0.13 | 0.11 | 12.1 | 0.71 / 0.69 | 0.82 / 0.82 | 0.60 / 0.56 | 0.78 / 0.71 |
| Merge TIES d = 0.5 | 0.043 | 0.73 | 0.057 | 0.084 | 0.19 | 0.14 | 17.2 | 0.73 / 0.69 | 0.75 / 0.73 | 0.73 / 0.65 | 0.84 / 0.69 |

Reading:
- The two experts are built the same way and look the same: 0.035–0.036% of B's norm overall, change concentrated in attention (0.65%), router (0.15–0.17%) and LM head, expert MLPs nearly untouched, 13% of weights changed. Their deltas share a direction (cosine 0.21 overall, 0.37 in attention, 0.38 at the LM head) while their expert-MLP changes are nearly independent (0.06), consistent with a common change in how the model answers (both experts start using their reasoning block on far more prompts) on top of domain-specific MLP changes.
- The mixed SFT arms move the weights most (0.17–0.18% overall, 55–56% of weights changed, expert MLPs 0.38–0.40%), 5× more than the experts whose text they train on, and in a direction almost orthogonal to both experts' deltas (cosine ≈0.02 overall and in the expert MLPs; 0.06 in attention). Only the LM head aligns (0.40–0.51).
- MOPD moves the weights a quarter as much as the SFT arms (0.045% overall, 25% of weights changed), again nearly orthogonal to the experts (0.05–0.13), with the LM head moving against both experts (−0.14 / −0.15). It recovers both experts' scores anyway.
- The merges are, by construction, the experts' deltas: TA 0.5 is their average (cosine 0.69–0.71 with each, magnitude 0.031%), TIES keeps the larger of the two per weight (0.043%, attention 0.73%). They sit far from where the trained arms end up (cosine between merge and arm deltas not computed here).
- Net: four different weight changes, differing in size by 5× and nearly orthogonal in direction, all land within a few points of the experts on both domains. The transfer is not a recovery of the expert's parameters; it is a re-learning of the behaviour from a different starting direction, which is also why the arms' off-domain scores (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA-D, IFEval) do not simply track the experts'.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights (two values = vs E / vs E₂). Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up on the delta-direction question: is the MOPD update "nearly orthogonal" to the expert update, or aligned beyond chance?

## Method

Deltas against the student B (`Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ fdc3c3c5) for expert E (CruxEval, step 272), expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro, step 254), the MOPD update (step 100) and the two mixed SFT arms (plain step 803, RS step 727). Three measures per component: cosine, sign agreement on weights changed in both, and subspace overlap, the share of a delta's energy inside the reference delta's top-k singular directions per matrix (k holding 50% of the reference energy), against two nulls: a random k-dim subspace and the reference delta with entries permuted within each matrix. The run reproduces the cosines posted above exactly. Script: `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_subspace.py` on branch `task/239` (4c99d4d9a4).

## Result

Overlap with E's half-energy subspace, as a multiple of the random null:

| Component | E₂ (peer expert) | MOPD | plain SFT | RS-SFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attention | 3.4× | 3.5× | 2.4× | 2.4× |
| Expert MLPs | 1.5× | 1.6× | 1.3× | 1.3× |
| Shared experts | 3.9× | 3.4× | 1.7× | 1.8× |
| Router | 2.0× | 2.8× | 1.7× | 1.6× |
| LM head | 295× | 198× | 397× | 407× |

Cosine and sign agreement with E, all weights: E₂ 0.21 / 0.55; MOPD 0.049 / 0.56; plain SFT 0.021 / 0.53; RS-SFT 0.023 / 0.53. In attention MOPD reaches 0.10 / 0.68 against E₂'s 0.38 / 0.71.

## Reading

- Cosine 0.05 over 6.7e10 weights is about 12,000 chance SDs (1/√n = 3.9e-6), so "beyond chance" is a weak bar. The informative controls are the SFT arms (same student, same prompts, same expert texts) and the peer expert.
- Against those controls, MOPD shares direction with the experts more than the SFT arms do, in every component except the LM head, and relative to the random null it sits close to the peer expert in attention and expert MLPs. The permuted null equals the random null everywhere, so the excess comes from the experts' dominant singular directions, not from their entry distribution.
- The shared part is small in energy: 0.24% of MOPD's update lies along E's delta, and 16% inside E's half-energy subspace against 10% for a random subspace. The posted conclusion stands: the transfer is mostly a different weight change that reaches the same behaviour.
- The LM head reverses the pattern: the SFT arms align strongly with the experts there (cos 0.40 to 0.51), while MOPD moves inside the same narrow top directions with the opposite sign (cos −0.14, sign agreement 0.39).
- None of the deltas is rank-1: participation ratios are 20 to 90 directions per matrix. The experts' attention deltas are the most concentrated (top-10 directions hold 80% of their energy); MOPD's is more spread (39%), the SFT arms' more still (24%).

## Limits

Correlational geometry only; no ablation, so no causal claim about the recovered scores. Cross-step self-consistency of the MOPD direction could not be measured because only step 100 exists. The bf16 exports hide changes below half an ulp, so every measure covers only what survived rounding.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
The agent above put some numbers together for "how orthogonal" the task vectors really are for each experiment arm. This is related to @penfever 's [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6201304545) about how the Frobenius norm of the task vector for MOPD is significantly smaller than SFT's.

However, I realized something else that I put in the experiment setup but forgot about: **The MOPD arm's batch size was effectively 16x higher than the SFT arm's with the same LR and fewer steps** . This might explain the whole difference. Specifically, they were "prompt matched", with each epoch seeing 3200 unique prompts / epoch. Specifically:

* SFT had 16 demonstration rows / step
  *  x 200 steps / epoch x 4 epochs = 12800 rollouts
  *  LR 1e-6
* MOPD had 64 prompts x 4 student rollouts / step x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 3200 prompts
  * x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 25600 rollouts 
  * LR 1e-6

As for why, at the time:
* We had known SFT runs on Snowball that used a 1e-6 LR, and I think even after doing sweeps in #10213 , that seems to be a good LR for this class of experiments
* We had existing M/OPD experiments under the proof-of-life experiments that used the 256 rollouts + 1e-6 LR
* MOPD needed more rollouts / batch to keep it from being as rollout-constrained
* MOPD by construction would see more unique sequences / epoch anyways if they started with the same dataset. 

Either way, we can do an experiment increasing MOPD LR to 4e-6, computed by sqrt(MOPD batch  / SFT batch) ( 1e-6) = 4 * 1e-6.

We'll also run for 4 epochs. This will give us a better sense of whether MOPD was under-stepped. 

Another difference I should note that won't change: MOPD is running using Megatron (our SkyRL setup), SFT is using Levanter

| Arm, checkpoint (updates) | H100-h | trained tokens | MMLU-Pro subset | CruxEval in / out |

| B (start) | 0 | 0 | 44.5 | 55.4 / 57.75 |
| Mixed plain SFT 201 / 402 / 603 / 804 | 50.5 / 77.4 / 104.4 / 131.4 | 2.8 / 5.7 / 8.5 / 11.3M | 61.0 / 62.8 / 60.9 / 62.4 | 69.5 / 66.75; 71.1 / 71.5; 79.25 / 73.4; 75.4 / 71.5 |

| E₂ (MMLU-Pro expert) / E (CruxEval expert) | 60.6 / 35.9 | 2.2 / 1.8M | 66.4 / – | – / 79.4, 71.4 |

How the numbers are built:
- **H100-hours.** Each arm's measured training-gang allocation, pro-rated by updates.
- **SFT arms.** Each carries both demo pools from step 0: E's (14.6 H100-h, reused from #9920) and E₂'s (8.9).
- **MOPD.** Each checkpoint carries its export job (about 14 H100-h). Measured allocation-to-checkpoint for MOPD, as a cross-check: ≈317 / ≈531 H100-h.
- **Trained tokens.** As in #9920: SFT from the row manifests × epochs, MOPD from per-update scored tokens.
- **Excluded.** Evaluations, building the experts, and the evicted plain attempt (14.2 H100-h).

Reading:
- **The arms reach different targets.** RS-SFT reaches E₂'s MMLU-Pro subset level at update 546 (93.7 H100-h); MOPD never does (best 65.0). MOPD reaches E's CruxEval input level at update 50 (292.8 H100-h); neither SFT arm does (best 78.75 / 79.25).
- **Matched GPU-hours.** Both SFT runs ended (117 and 131 H100-h) before MOPD's first checkpoint (292.8). At the SFT arms' final cost, a straight line from B to MOPD update 50 puts MOPD at about 53 MMLU-Pro and 65–67 / 65–66 CruxEval. That is an interpolation, not a measurement.
- **Trained tokens.** MOPD trains on 7–9× more tokens than the SFT arms; most of them (56.7M) come in its first epoch.

Caveats:
- This is not a matched-compute experiment; the arms differ in optimizer, batch geometry and verifier access.
- Single passes unless marked.
- MOPD's W&B history logged 99 of 100 updates.
- The RS demo selector used a different MMLU-Pro answer rule from the evaluator, which affects 1% of its demos.

Same student, teachers, prompts, rollout settings, evaluator, configs and seed; checkpoints at 50, 100, 150 and 200. Paired deltas use the per-question difference against the 1e-6 run at the matching step (its last step, 100, for steps 150 and 200) with a bootstrap interval.

**Reading**
- No target gain at any step: every MMLU-Pro subset interval contains 0, and CruxEval stays within about ±2 points. Steps 150 and 200 are no better than step 100.
- Held-out cost that persists: IFEval −9 to −11, MATH500 −3 to −5, GSM8K −3. GPQA returns to the 1e-6 level by step 200 (within noise), and held-out MMLU-Pro ends slightly above it (+1.4 [+0.5, +2.4] at step 200, after −1.0 at step 150).
- Dynamics match the 1e-6 run but arrive earlier: policy entropy rose about 20 updates sooner and rollouts were about 3x shorter at the same update.

issues.body: ## TL;DR (Conclusion) **Final, 2026-10-24: stopped and written up.** No SFT method beat plain SFT by enough to matter; the source of the traces decided the result. See the [summary comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213#issuecomment-6618401658) and the [paper](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/f0ad30e1ebafa432c3af144aa6faad76119a6c97/logbooks/10213-sft-shootout/agentic-sft-shootout.pdf). The design-stage text below is kept as written. Design stage, 2026-10-16. We compare five supervised fine-tuning (SFT) mechanisms for agentic coding on one base, one task pool, one teacher and one supervised-token budget: plain SFT (one accepted demonstration per task), rejection-sampled SFT with resampling across epochs, relay SFT (#10027), recovery SFT, and plateau dropping (#10028). The earlier transfer experiments (#9920, #9984) compared plain SFT, rejection-sampled SFT, on-policy distillation and weight merging on non-agentic tasks; this experiment moves to agentic tasks under the eval policy (#10197) and drops merging and distillation. Nothing has trained yet except a learning-rate sweep of the control, which is in progress. **Eval policy results (updated 2026-11-06):** the full benchmark tables for this experiment's candidates are in [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213#issuecomment-6665514128) and are updated in place after each reviewed delta. ## Question Which mechanism, if any, improves Snowball v0 on SWE-bench Verified and the terminal benchmarks over plain SFT at equal supervised tokens, without losing retention on GSM8K, BFCL-Parity and GPQA-Diamond. ## Fixed choices - Base: Snowball v0 = `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12` @ `4eeb756b`. v0 carries a diluted DARE graft of the allkimi relay SFT, so relay's lift reads smaller than it would on a pre-graft checkpoint; this is accepted because the question is what improves the release. - Task pool: about 2,200 TMax environments (`allenai/TMax-SFT-16.5K`, tasks.zip) and about 2,100 SWE-smith tasks sampled from the Harbor packages in `DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s`, stratified by repository, SWE-bench Verified repositories removed, decontaminated through DataKit against SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and TBLite 2.0. Selection is outcome-blind. SWE-smith packages receive a git-history strip before the agent phase (#10212). - Harness per task family, matching the policy's scoring agent: TMax under Terminus-2, SWE-smith under mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, both in Harbor under the policy pins. - Teacher: GLM 5.3 through the internal inference service, 8 attempts per task, verified by each task's tests. v0 is never sampled except in relay, where it starts each task and GLM continues after a trigger (format error, context budget, completion claim). - Recipe, shared by every arm: the #9984 comparison-arm settings (AdamW, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, clip 1.0, router bias frozen, batch 16 at 32k context, constant learning rate, loss averaged over supervised tokens), 3 epochs, replay of general SFT data (`nemotron_sft_v3`, reasoning kept) at one quarter of the agentic budget. The learning rate comes from the sweep below. ## Arms and token matching B is the supervised-token count of the plain arm: the first passing attempt per task with at least one pass, one trajectory per task. Every arm trains on B agentic tokens plus the same replay slice for the same number of optimizer steps. - Plain SFT (control): as above. - RS-multi: identical task slots to plain; when a task recurs in a later epoch, a different passing attempt is used. Measures demonstration diversity at a fixed budget. - Relay (#10027): v0's own turns stay in context with no loss; GLM's turns are trained; passing episodes subsampled to B. Episodes with no teacher turn are dropped. - Recovery (phase 2): the plain trajectories; 20% receive one or two synthetic failed turns re-rendered in v0's measured error styles plus the real harness error, inserted through the parser; injections carry no loss, so the budget equals B by construction. Waits on a validated injection generator. - Plateau dropping (#10028, phase 2): the plain trajectories; tokens whose loss has plateaued lose gradient; matched on optimizer steps, with gradient-carrying tokens reported. Waits on the trainer. Phase 1 is plain, RS-multi and relay. ## Evaluation Every arm, including plain, runs the retention gate (GSM8K, BFCL-Parity, GPQA-Diamond) and the agentic endpoint (SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1, TBLite 2.0) under the policy's trial counts and pins. An arm passes when it has no decisive loss against plain on the gate and a decisive win over plain on at least one agentic benchmark with no decisive loss on the others, where decisive is the policy's rule (gap above 1.96 times the combined task-level standard error, each scaled by 1/sqrt(0.9)). One policy run resolves gaps of roughly 4 to 5 points on SWE-bench Verified and 8 to 10 on the terminal benchmarks; unresolved arms are reported with intervals and not promoted. Passing arms, plain and v0 go to the 23-benchmark tournament. ## Learning-rate sweep of the control Running now, on pilot data (existing Qwen3.6-27B TMax traces and Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith traces, history-reading trials removed), four runs from v0 at 3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6 and 1e-5, 3 epochs, recipe otherwise fixed. Screens per run: held-out validation loss on 5% of tasks, GSM8K, BFCL-Parity, SWE-bench Verified random-100 and a 100-task TBLite subset. Decision rule, fixed in advance: among rates with no decisive retention loss against v0, the best equal-weight mean of the two agentic screens; ties to the smaller rate. The chosen rate is confirmed once on the real plain-arm data and then frozen for all arms. ## Budget Core (sweep, generation, phase 1, tournament) about 3,700 to 4,000 H100-hours; phase 2 adds about 2,400, of which 1,700 is an optional 20-epoch plateau comparison. GLM generation runs on the internal service and sandbox CPU and is outside the GPU budget. ## Status and next steps - Pilot dataset and learning-rate sweep: in progress. - Task pool, decontamination and package fix: in progress. - Harness bring-up, one-task dry runs, a 200-task-per-family pass-rate pilot and a relay dry run: in progress. The full 8-attempt generation waits on their results. - Then: phase-1 training, first-stage evaluation, tournament for passers; phase 2 when its code exists. Design notes and diagrams are kept in the maintainer's notes and will be attached as results land. ## Decision log - 2026-10-15: scope cut to SFT only; merging and on-policy distillation dropped. Base set to Snowball v0. - 2026-10-16: one harness per task family following the policy's scoring agents; GLM 5.3 as the single teacher with regenerated traces instead of reusing Kimi and Qwen traces; RS arm redefined as resampling across epochs after the token-budgeted variant was found to re-weight tasks; task eligibility defined by teacher success only; unfiltered-SFT control dropped; primary endpoint set to the agentic benchmarks with the tournament secondary; git-history leak found in the SWE-smith packages and a strip added to the pool build.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Teacher generation bring-up: one-task dry runs

## TL;DR

GLM 5.3 now runs end to end in both harnesses (Harbor `016dd78b`, Daytona sandboxes, run from cw-us-east-02a):
- TMax under Terminus-2, with the 65,536 / 16,384 limits from the policy;
- SWE-smith under the mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 adapter, with a 32,768-token window.

**The adapter question is answered.** The mini-swe-agent adapter runs a raw SWE-smith Harbor package unchanged, and the dry-run trace fit inside 32k (largest prompt 13.4k tokens). One trace says nothing about the length distribution; the pilot will measure it.

**The GLM pass on SWE-smith read the fix from git history** (#10212). Before the SWE-smith pass-rate pilot, the packages need the history-stripped repair.

**The pilot has not started.** It waits on a capacity confirmation for the GLM service.

## Per trial

| | TMax `task_000000_5c5b0938` | SWE-smith `swesmith-00003` |
|---|---|---|
| Reward | 0 in the first run, 1 in a rerun | 1 in both runs |
| Model calls | 4 | 16 to 17 |
| Prompt tokens (total / largest) | 9.3k to 10.1k / 3.7k | 145k to 156k (about 93% prefix-cached) / 13.4k |
| Completion tokens (reasoning) | 5.1k to 6.2k (4.2k to 5.2k) | 3.4k to 3.6k (0.5k to 0.8k) |
| Model time | 39 s | 16 s |
| Trial wall time | 42 to 93 s (environment build 3 to 45 s) | 74 to 80 s (verifier 20 to 25 s) |

## Effective generation settings

Both clients send only `model` and `max_tokens=16384`, so GLM runs on the service defaults. GLM 5.3's template then renders `Reasoning Effort: Max`.

Every request is logged by an in-cluster proxy. The log records the settings as sent and the full reply, reasoning included. The proxy also serves `/tokenize` with the `zai-org/GLM-5.3` tokenizer, because the mini-swe-agent context limiter needs it and the relay does not provide it. Its token counts matched the service on every request.

## Transcripts

Both harnesses write Harbor ATIF trajectories:
- **Terminus-2:** each step's message is the JSON action, and the reasoning is in `reasoning_content`.
- **mini-swe-agent:** native `bash` tool calls with `{returncode, output}` observations, but the trajectory **drops GLM's reasoning**. Training rows are therefore rebuilt from the proxy log, which keeps it. That rebuild checks clean on both dry runs.

## What the agent can see

Measured with an oracle-agent probe during the agent phase:

| | TMax (converted) | SWE-smith (raw package) |
|---|---|---|
| `/tests` | absent | absent |
| `/solution` | absent | absent |
| Other task files | none | none |
| Git history | no repository | 944 branches, including `main` and the full history |

The SWE-smith dry-run pass used that history: it ran `git show 614b134:<file>`, then checked its edit against that file. Details are in #10212.

## Other findings

- **TMax is not in Harbor format** in `tasks.zip`. The pool converts it with TMax's own `convert_to_harbor.py` at `hamishivi/tmax@6d3d606c`, minus 181 environments with hidden verifier assets, giving 2,019 tasks.
- **The dry-run TMax task looks flawed.** It runs an OpenMP parallel loop over the outer LU loop with 4 threads, while the test expects the sequential determinant. The task failed once and passed once.

## Next

- **TMax pilot:** 200 tasks x 2 attempts, seed 20261016, drawn uniformly from 1,963 eligible tasks (the pool minus #202's held-out ids). Staged; starts when capacity is confirmed.
- **SWE-smith pilot:** 200 x 2, stratified by repository, on the history-stripped packages.
- **Relay dry run:** 20 tasks per family, with v0 served by the policy serving config. GLM takes over on these triggers:
  - format error: GLM writes one repair turn;
  - context budget at 0.75 of the window: GLM continues to the end;
  - completion claim: v0's reply is withheld and logged, and GLM continues to the end.

Run folders: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/generation/dryrun/{tmax-dry1,tmax-dry2,swe-dry3,swe-dry4,visibility1}`

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Relay rounds broken by a preempted student server ([#10237](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10237)).

**Affected rounds**
- TMax relay shard-02 round 1: 198 of 200 trials errored, 14:33-15:13 UTC on 2026-10-17. Moved to `traces/tmax-relay/shard-02/round-1.failed-0a6b03ad`; it will be rerun. It was never published.
- SWE-smith relay shard-00 round 3: 85 of 97 trials errored, from about 08:29 UTC. Its 32 valid rows are published; trials that raised without a GLM reply don't count as relay runs.

I'm checking every other round for a student preemption and will post the full list.

**Cause.** In relay mode, the v0 student runs as a child inference job. When that job was preempted, Iris rescheduled it on another host. The relay proxy kept calling the address resolved once at startup (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py:682`). Every student call then failed with `httpx.ConnectError`, the agents got HTTP 500, and Harbor still exited 0.

**Fix** (`task/212` @ [`174906474a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/174906474a8039d1ff8989e8f6d53103242cfec1)):
- On a connection error, the proxy looks up the student's current address and retries for up to 20 minutes.
- The proxy logs its own failures, which used to go unlogged.
- A run fails, with no `_SUCCESS`, when more than 20% of its trials raise without a reply.

The relay lanes are being resubmitted on this commit.

comments.body:
🤖 Decisions for the next data round (v7), 2026-10-19.

1. Regenerate the GLM 5.3 pool at a lower reasoning effort. The max-effort traces caused both phase-1 defects: long reasoning used up the 30k generation window (so half of the passing SWE-smith attempts never reached the submit step) and taught a style that times out TBLite. GLM 5.3's chat template exposes only `low`, `high` and max (`medium` renders as max, and `high` reasoned to the token cap like max in a probe), so a pilot of 200 TMax and 200 SWE-smith tasks x 2 samples at `low` and `high` is running (launched 21:01 UTC) to measure pass rate, clean-pass rate, per-turn reasoning and context use against the max-effort pool. The full k=8 regeneration on pool v5, plus relay rounds, follows at the chosen setting with the same gates.
2. Select demonstrations by clean completion: an attempt counts only if it passed and ended with the agent's own finish (mini-swe-agent submit, Terminus-2 `task_complete`). On the max-effort traces this keeps 919 of 1,995 SWE-smith tasks and 1,475 of 1,914 TMax tasks; the lower-effort traces should keep more.
3. Switch the base to Snowball v0.1 (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14`, selected in #10283 under the same policy). Same architecture, tokenizer and template as v0, and without v0's relay SFT graft, so it is a cleaner base for the relay arm. The relay student becomes v0.1 and v0.1 reference screens will be run. The LR sweep result (1e-6, 3 epochs) is carried over rather than repeated.
4. Rebuild all five arms on the new rows, retrain and screen them. The v5 arms above remain the max-effort finding.

Recovery SFT implementation check: the owner obtained the original recovery generation code; the mechanism matches ours (injection points, 1–3 attempts, Terminus-2 reply template and parser, teacher-authored failed turns, masking). Two rendering details from it are adopted (varied renders per error style; streaks of the same style, with rates measured on v0's own trajectories: 56.6% same style, 0% identical); we keep trained tokens equal to plain's.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Update 2026-10-22: every SFT arm trained on the GLM 5.3 traces scores below its parent on the agentic screens. Two next steps: re-run the cheap arms on the contributor (Kimi/Qwen) traces, and check the learning rate on the real rows.**

## Results on the GLM 5.3 traces

Screens are SWE-bench Verified random-100 and the TBLite 100-task subset (solved out of 100; TBLite timeouts count as failures), GSM8K and BFCL-Parity for retention. "Composite" is our screening mean (SWE + TBLite)/2, shown as a range when trials were unscored for infrastructure reasons; it is a bound, not a confidence interval. HIGH and LOW are the GLM reasoning-effort settings used to generate the traces; rows are token-matched per arm.

| model | parent | rows | SWE-bench r100 (submits) | TBLite-100 | GSM8K | BFCL | composite | EvalDash |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| --- |
| parent v0.1 | – | – | 26 (36) | 23 | 91.1 | 32/123 | 24.5-25.0 |  |
| plain | v0.1 | HIGH | 13 (4) | 8 | 92.3 | 67/123 | 10.5-11.5 |  |
| plain | v0.1 | LOW | 17 (27) | 12 | 91.7 | 55/121 | 14.5-18.0 | [EvalDash](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs?model=v7-plain-low-v01-20261020) |
| relay | v0.1 | LOW | 25 (25) | 15 | 92.9 | 64/123 | 20.0-21.0 | [EvalDash](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs?model=v7-relay-low-v01-20261021) |
| parent v0 | – | – | 33 (56) | 20 | 85.2 | 27/122 | 26.5-27.0 |  |
| plain | v0 | HIGH | 17 (3) | 9 | 87.7 | 44/122 | 13.0-17.5 |  |
| plain, cut to the relay arm's token count | v0 | HIGH | 13 (6) | 11 | 91.1 | 54/123 | 12.0-12.5 |  |
| RS-multi | v0 | HIGH | 11 (6) | 10 | 89.9 | 41/123 | 10.5-11.0 | [EvalDash](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs?model=v7-rs-multi-v0-20261021) |
| recovery | v0 | HIGH | 12 (4) | 9 | 88.5 | 48/123 | 10.5-11.0 | [EvalDash](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs?model=v7-recovery-v0-20261021) |
| relay | v0 | HIGH | 13 (1) | 14 | 89.0 | 48/123 | 13.5-14.0 |  |
| plateau dropping | v0 | HIGH | 14 (6) | 13 | 89.8 | 49/123 | 13.5 |  |

What the data say:
- Every arm is below its parent on SWE-bench and TBLite and above it on GSM8K and BFCL. The regression is specific to the agentic tasks.
- Paired per-task differences on the frozen task lists (task bootstrap, 95%): no HIGH-row method differs from plain on either screen (SWE-bench -3 to -6 [about -13, +4]; TBLite 0 to +3 [about -6, +9]). Relay on the LOW rows beats plain on the LOW rows on SWE-bench by +8 [+1, +16], the only method-versus-twin interval that excludes zero; on TBLite +1 [-6, +7]. Every student is below its parent on SWE-bench (HIGH-row arms -13 to -22, intervals exclude zero; LOW relay -1 [-10, +8]) and most are below on TBLite.
- Relay on the LOW rows is therefore the strongest arm (25 SWE-bench vs the parent's 26), with the caveat that its recipe differs from plain's (963 vs 675 updates at equal tokens, student prefix masked) and that LOW rows hold 11.6M supervised tokens per epoch against HIGH's 19.4M.
- Mechanism, measured on trajectories: students keep the rows' per-step style (about 120 tokens per step, same command mix) but take about twice the rows' steps, run into the 32k window (75-97% of episodes) and rarely submit (HIGH-trained 3-6%, LOW-trained about 25%, parents 36-56%). Submitting is where the score comes from.
- The two parents are not distinguishable on the frozen task lists: paired SWE-bench difference v0 minus v0.1 = +7 [-2, +16], TBLite -3 [-12, +6] (task bootstrap). Of the 49 TBLite tasks where v0.1 timed out, v0 solved 3, so v0.1's timeouts are mostly hard tasks, not lost score (#10338: tripling the limit changed its score by one task).

Limits: one run per arm, 100 tasks per screen (about 4 points of standard error), TBLite timeout-bound for every student.

## Next step 1: the same cheap arms on the contributor traces

The one run of this recipe that beat its parent was the learning-rate sweep's 1e-6 run on the pilot traces (Qwen3.6-27B TMax episodes and Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith episodes, the data the contributors' original experiments used): composite 31.0-32.0 against v0's 26.5-27.0, TBLite 29 vs 20. That run used the sweep's sampler and exposure, not the arm recipe, so it is suggestive, not a control. The pilot rows also look different from the GLM rows: 14 steps per episode at 246 tokens per step with 28% reasoning tokens (HIGH: 25 steps, 120 tokens, 39%), and they are in Terminus-2 format, which never contains the mini-swe-agent submit command, yet that student kept 40% submits.

Plan: convert the pilot traces to the arm row format and train plain, RS-multi and recovery from v0.1 at 1e-6 under the arm recipe, plus plain from v0 as the bridge to the sweep. v0.1 is the base because it carries no relay graft and v0 was trained on about half of the pilot SWE tasks through the relay data grafted into it. Known limits: the Kimi SWE set has one trajectory per task, so RS-multi runs on TMax only; recovery needs an error style for Qwen's native tool calls; about 1,500 pilot SWE tasks have only the pilot's own decontamination check. Target: plain results within a day of the rows, the other two a day later.

## Next step 2: learning rate on the real rows

The sweep tied 3e-7, 1e-6 and 3e-6 on the pilot rows and 1e-6 was frozen without the planned confirmation on real plain rows. Two checks are running: plain SFT on the LOW v0 rows at 3e-7, paired against the 1e-6 twin (same rows, parent and schedule), to test whether gentler updates preserve more of the parent; and a screen of the HIGH plain v0.1 epoch-2 checkpoint against its final, as an update-dose check. A higher rate is not excluded but is the less likely direction given the sweep.

Also in flight: plain, relay and plateau on the LOW rows from v0, and RS-multi and recovery on the LOW rows from v0.1, to complete the LOW comparison on both parents. Models so far are on the Hub under `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-SFT-Shootout-*` (private). Design: [SFT comparison doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/13duCN6reb7KVLhBi8TszTL1EYKeaV3SEMQhl9IJCZSM/edit).

Paired per-task differences (task bootstrap, 95%):

| comparison | SWE-bench | TBLite |

| contribshared − lowshared (the matched pair) | **+26 [+17, +36]** | **+9 [+1, +17]** |
| contribshared − parent v0.1 | **+10 [+1, +19]** | −5 [−15, +4] |

What the data say:
- On identical tasks, GLM LOW rows push the student far below the parent, and contributor rows lift it above the parent on SWE-bench. The contributor-side +10 is the first gap against the parent that clears noise.

A lower learning rate (3e-7: SWE −7 [−13, −1] against 1e-6) and an earlier checkpoint (2 of 3 epochs: +5 [−4, +13]) also did not rescue the GLM rows.

Not tested: what remains between the row sets is the teacher (GLM 5.3 against Kimi/Qwen) and the harness format. Our GLM rows use each eval's own action protocol; the contributor rows use the other one.

Trace decontamination: the trained trace text was checked against the 100 SWE-bench gold and test patches and the 100 TBLite tests and solutions. There were 3 flags, all TBLite, all generic code (imports, a file-reading loop). Nothing was excluded.

Cost of these runs: 184.9 H100-h training and 106.4 H100-h screens. Documented total for the experiment: about 6,070 H100-h (a partial subtotal, not an invoice).

comments.author: karansag
comments.body: 🤖 **Summary: no SFT method beat plain SFT by enough to matter; the source of the traces decided the result. The experiment is stopped and written up.** ## Data We took 2,200 TMAX and 2,100 SWE-smith tasks and regenerated traces using GLM 5.3. This way, both would have a consistent teacher. We also ran these traces using the corresponding eval harness under policy. For SWE-smith, this was `mini-swe-agent`, and for TMax, it was `Terminus-2`. Relay pools were also constructed similarly, starting with a base Snowball and handing off to GLM 5.3 Note that GLM 5.3 was tried with different effort levels (as per comments above). We used the contributor rows directly (SWE-smith + TMax under Kimi 2.5 / Qwen3.6-27B) for both pilot sweeps and as a final run to assess the impact of our data after a negative with GLM 5.3 traces. ## What we did We compared plain SFT, rejection-sampled SFT (RS-multi), relay, recovery and plateau dropping for agentic coding on Snowball v0 and v0.1. The task pool was about 2,200 TMax and 2,100 SWE-smith tasks. Traces came from GLM 5.3 at three reasoning efforts, then from the contributor traces (Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith, Qwen3.6-27B TMax). Screens: SWE-bench Verified random-100, TBLite-100, GSM8K and BFCL-Parity. ## What we found 1. **Every arm trained on GLM 5.3 traces scored below its parent** on SWE-bench and TBLite, while gaining on GSM8K and BFCL. The students took about twice the steps of their training traces, ran into the 32k context limit in most SWE-bench episodes and rarely submitted. 2. **Methods mattered little.** Only relay on LOW rows beat plain SFT (SWE-bench +8 [+1, +16]), and it still trailed its parent. On contributor rows, plain, RS-multi, recovery and plateau dropping were indistinguishable. 3. **The rows mattered most.** With the same 1,432 tasks, parent and recipe, contributor rows beat GLM LOW rows by SWE-bench +26 [+17, +36] and TBLite +9 [+1, +17]. The contributor side also beat parent v0.1 on SWE-bench by +10 [+1, +19]. 4. **Less GLM exposure did not help.** A lower learning rate, an earlier checkpoint and a smaller subset all stayed below the parent. ## Hypotheses (untested) Why the GLM arms lost while the contributor rows gained, and why collaborators got large SFT gains from Kimi and Qwen traces on a weaker Snowball parent ([blog post, 2026-10-21](https://lukedhlee.github.io/blog/2026/10/21/turning-snowball-into-a-coding-agent/)). Ordered by how much evidence we have. 1. **Teacher traces.** GLM 5.3 episodes were long, reasoning-heavy and often ended at the context limit; the students copied that. Kimi and Qwen traces did not. The matched pair (+26 SWE-bench on the same tasks) is the strongest evidence we have for anything. A different teacher on the same tasks and format would test it. 2. **SFT alone does not fix action behavior.** The collaborators' best results came from SFT then RL; their trace analysis found RL cut invalid actions from about 80% to 2% and taught the model to submit its best effort instead of running out of context. Those are exactly the failures of our GLM students. RL from a shootout checkpoint would test it. 3. **Training stack.** The collaborators report that an early relay advantage disappeared after correcting training precision and MoE expert capacity. Our arms trained before #10492 made expert capacity configurable; at the default capacity with expert parallelism, overflow tokens are dropped silently (seen later in the identity work). Whether the shootout arms dropped tokens is not known. It can be checked by replaying one saved run with drop counting. 4. **Eval protocol.** Our screens use 32k context, 1,800 s and one trial; the collaborators use 64k, a 3x timeout and three repeats. Our GLM students produce longer episodes, so our limits may punish them more than a longer protocol would. The 65k-context and 5,400 s checks ran on the parent only, not on a student. 5. **Parent headroom.** Their parent was the general-SFT 09-21 checkpoint (12.8% SWE-bench under Terminus-2). Ours were merged and RL-trained parents, and v0 already carries a relay graft trained on 1,012 of the same Kimi trajectories. Demonstrations may have less to add to our parents. 6. **Harness format.** Our GLM traces were recorded in each eval's own harness and hurt that eval; the contributor traces were recorded the other way round and did not. Training in the eval's own format may overwrite the parent's behavior there. But the collaborators' Kimi SWE traces are Terminus-2 format and their SWE eval runs under Terminus-2, and that worked, so this is weaker than it first looked. Format is confounded with the teacher. Re-recording GLM traces in the other format (about 125 H100-h) would separate them. 7. **Training dose.** We trained 3 epochs at 1e-6. The collaborators' RL started from a 7-epoch SFT model, and their RL ablation found more epochs helped until overfitting. This would not rescue the GLM arms, which got worse, but the contributor rows were never trained past 3 epochs. Cost: about 6,070 H100-h documented. ## Records - Paper (15 pages, PDF, with the three experiment diagrams): [agentic-sft-shootout.pdf](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/f0ad30e1ebafa432c3af144aa6faad76119a6c97/logbooks/10213-sft-shootout/agentic-sft-shootout.pdf), with a short [notebook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/f0ad30e1ebafa432c3af144aa6faad76119a6c97/logbooks/10213-sft-shootout/notebook.md) and the diagram sources in marin-logbooks. - Results by round: the comments above, last two dated 2026-10-22 and 2026-10-24. - Code: reusable parts in draft PRs #10255 (plateau dropping in `train_lm`), #10887 (recording relay proxy and trace rebuild) and #10888 (recovery rows). The rest of the experiment code is archived on marin-logbooks branches `codex/10213-sft-shootout-pr`, listed in the notebook. - Models: private `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-SFT-Shootout-*` repos on the Hub.
