issues.author: zoe110501
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Compare two-sided EMA gradient-Gram preconditioning on Delphi's 447M recipe. The implementation includes numerical tests, full-state checkpoint probes and experiment planning. The first baseline pilot is complete; tuned comparisons remain pending after a quarter-power host-memory failure.

## Description

For each matrix gradient G, maintain zero-initialized momentum M (beta1=0.95) and Gram EMAs L=EMA(GG^T), R=EMA(G^TG), initially beta2=0.99. Let A and B be the respective Grams divided by their mean eigenvalue, then regularized with epsilon I. A zero Gram uses identity. Apply the descent direction -A^-alpha polar(A^-alpha M B^-alpha) B^-alpha, where polar replaces positive singular values by one and leaves zero modes zero.

Compare alpha=0, 1/8, 1/4, 1/3 and 1/2. Across variants, hold constant architecture, tokenizer, data order, batch, context, schedule shape, parameter routing, global clipping, nonmatrix AdamW, precision, weight decay, full-matrix geometry, Gram refresh at every update, and the five-step production polar approximation. Alpha=0 accumulates Grams passively.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine whether alpha=1/4 improves held-out loss over alpha=1/2 and alpha=0 after independently tuning learning rates. Use per-matrix norm-matched checkpoint probes and offline SVD comparisons to assess magnitude and approximation effects.

## Status

The workflow implements:
- 30 initial pilots of approximately 250M tokens each: three learning rates and two relative ridges (1e-4, 1e-2) for each nonzero exponent, and six learning rates for alpha=0. LR centers are explicit per exponent. Expand every edge-winning grid before selection.
- Final validation-loss selection with locked hyperparameters and a common loss target before confirmation.
- Fresh approximately 1.2B-token confirmations with paired initialization/data seeds 0, 42 and 62746 for alpha=0, 1/4 and 1/2, plus the overall pilot-winning exponent if outside that set.
- Complete checkpoints near 10%, 50% and 90% of one reference run. Probe identical momentum/Gram states on independent held-out batches over a common step grid; report batch-level deltas, standard deviations and standard errors.
- Offline production-polar versus SVD diagnostics on selected attention and MLP matrices, online W&B, incremental local logs, peak-memory snapshots and XProf traces.
- Conditional comparisons of horizons 100/1,000/10,000 updates and the existing 998M/5B-token recipe after reviewing reproducibility.

The alpha=0 pilot completed 7,630 updates and 250,019,840 tokens, with final C4 English validation loss 3.91522193 nats. Iris and W&B report successful completion; final checkpoint metadata and the metric tail were verified. Observed host-memory peak was 28.5996 GiB. The alpha=1/4 pilot failed from host OOM at zero-based step 7, before validation, with observed host peak 62.9297 GiB against 64 GiB. The user authorized the 128 GiB recovery, which Iris accepted at 23:42:58 UTC on October 30 as `ema-gram-20-quarter-pilot-128g-20261030`, version `2026.10.30.23`. The recovery now trains on TPU v4 with fresh online W&B run ending `d8755c4b4082`, reaching step 60 at 07:17 UTC on October 31. Observed host peak is 91.7295 GiB and early steady steps take about 40 seconds; the planned profile will isolate nonzero-alpha cost before sweep expansion. The research notebook preserves both attempts and the full exports. These results do not establish a best exponent; tuning, confirmations and probes remain outstanding.

## Links

- [Delphi recipe and seed instructions](https://marin.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reproducibility/delphi-seed-repeats/)
- Earlier optimizer work: #6588, #6538, #6506 and #4919.
- Implementation: #10790. [Completed baseline W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/ema-gram-pilot-3e18-a0-seed0-a46345a749ca-2026.10.30.22-412aad49e64f).

## Decision Log

2026-10-30: Use the requested two-sided spectral Gram powers and keep all exponent controls fixed. The final results in #6588 showed that replacing an exact inverse square root with a saturating polynomial changed held-out loss; this motivates measuring approximation effects explicitly.

## Conclusion

Pending tuned pilots, paired confirmation, norm-matched probes and accelerator cost profiles. The final readout should include individual seed curves versus tokens and elapsed time, paired differences, common-target crossings, tuned LR/ridge choices, failures, memory, optimizer/decomposition/communication cost, and whether any advantage survives norm matching.

Execution and results are tracked in [marin-logbooks #20](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/20), with the published source, plans and notebook linked there. This issue continues to track the implementation in #10790.

🤖 Answering this issue's experiment questions from the completed seed0 campaign. **No failed longrun will be rerun.** The current instruction is to report the available evidence and mark the missing experiments; shutdown/runtime-packaging work is deferred.

[Full question-by-question answer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/48d81f8cd358b7194a6620cf6b54ccb40541669c/logbooks/20-ema-gram-polar/ali-question-answers.md), [evidence index](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/48d81f8cd358b7194a6620cf6b54ccb40541669c/logbooks/20-ema-gram-polar/ali-answer-evidence.json), and [existing curves and scientific findings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/48d81f8cd358b7194a6620cf6b54ccb40541669c/logbooks/20-ema-gram-polar/single-seed-findings.md). Execution history remains in [logbooks #20](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/20). Earlier one-sided Qwen3/BPB results in #6588 are separate evidence.

### 1. Does quarter power beat zero and half power after tuning?

**The recovered quarter-power endpoint is worse than alpha=0 and better than half power. It does not support superiority to both controls.**

| Alpha | Pilot-selected matrix LR | Ridge | Final C4 loss (nats) | Status |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 0 | 0.003535534 | 0.0001 | 3.792297 | Validated completion |

| 1/4 | 0.002 | 0.01 | 3.844011 | Failed execution; recovered local evaluation |
| 1/2 | 0.001 | 0.01 | 3.958380 | Failed execution; recovered local evaluation |

Quarter power is +0.051714 nats versus zero and −0.114369 versus half. Alpha=1/8 is −0.008272 versus zero. These are independently tuned configurations: 37 completed pilots selected LR/ridge before confirmation. Each pilot used 7,630 updates (250,019,840 tokens). The full runs used 37,335 updates, 1,223,393,280 tokens and the fixed HQ/code/math recipe. This is seed0 only, not cross-seed reproducibility or a byte-identical reproduction of the original Delphi data recipe.

The failed endpoints are supplementary recovered measurements, not validated completions. For alpha=1/4, 112 training-log steps still lack all five required loss/performance/LR fields; no values are imputed.

**Why alpha=1/4 failed:** cached evidence establishes a distributed shutdown failure: a 3/4 JAX barrier, tracker finalization blocked on process0, and W&B background completion abandoned after 120 seconds. One task records exit139/SIGSEGV; stderr also mentions signal6. The initiating cause and signal discrepancy remain unresolved. This does not establish optimizer divergence.

### 2. Does a direction advantage survive per-matrix norm matching?

The three checkpoint probes are complete. A direct paired analysis of their cached losses compares quarter power with zero/half on the same eight held-out batches:

| Reference update | Quarter lower than zero | Quarter lower than half |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 3,733 | 4/6 settings | 2/6 |
| 18,665 | 4/6 | 2/6 |
| 33,597 | 5/6 | 2/6 |

Six settings = two ridges × three common step sizes. These counts are descriptive, not independent wins or significance tests. Four hosts are replicas, not 32 samples. Across settings/stages, mean differences span −0.000488 to +0.000289 nats versus zero and −0.000137 to +0.000294 versus half. Per-contrast paired SEMs span 0.00002472–0.00013039 nats; [all 36 contrasts and eight batch differences each](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/48d81f8cd358b7194a6620cf6b54ccb40541669c/logbooks/20-ema-gram-polar/ali-norm-matched-contrasts.json) retain the corresponding uncertainty.

There is no consistent quarter-power advantage over both controls. At the late checkpoint, all 27 original perturbations increased mean loss versus leaving the checkpoint unchanged. These local tests do not establish a norm-matched full-training effect.

### 3. Could polar approximation explain quality?

Still open. Production-versus-SVD direction diagnostics cover two matrices × nine exponent/ridge settings × three checkpoints: cosine 0.863830–0.999752, relative error 0.022707–0.521354. The comparison changes only the polar method at fixed state/Gram powers. **It does not compare production-versus-SVD losses or training outcomes.**

### 4. What do token/time/compute measurements say?

First observed C4≤4.0 crossings, without interpolation:

| Alpha | Updates | Native hours | Device-hours |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 34,000 | 4.770 | 19.081 |
| 1/8 | 33,000 | 35.630 | 570.088 |
| 1/4, failed | 34,000 | 39.567 | 633.076 |
| 1/2, failed | 36,000 | 42.988 | 687.808 |

Native time includes compilation/evaluation and excludes queueing. Baseline used four v4 devices; nonzero runs used sixteen with a different model mesh. Consequently the 1/8-to-zero 7.47× time and 29.88× device-hour ratios describe these deployments, **not matched-hardware optimizer overhead**. Comparable peak memory and source-matched Gram/decomposition/communication cost attribution remain missing.

### Remaining experiments/evidence — conditional, none authorized or launched

- [ ] **Directional generalization:** fixed checkpoint/ridge/step comparisons on fresh disjoint held-out batches, retaining all paired differences.
- [ ] **Polar approximation's local loss effect:** same-state, norm-matched production-versus-exact-SVD perturbation losses on common fresh batches. Local effects alone would not prove the full-training cause.
- [ ] **Compute/memory attribution:** inspect matching cached traces first; if unavailable, a short same-source, same-topology profiling/memory experiment.
- [ ] **Cross-seed reproducibility, only if claimed:** new paired seeds using frozen pilot settings; outside the amended seed0 scope.
- [ ] **Horizon/998M follow-ups:** deferred; the original reproducibility gate is unmet.

Alpha=1/3 was included in pilots but was not the best-other exponent selected for confirmation. A full-budget 1/3 run would expand scope, not complete a missing prescribed cell. None of these gaps requires silently replacing the failed seed0 runs.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
When an evaluation serves a model from Hugging Face, the model weights are downloaded by the GPU serving job itself, as the first thing it does before starting vLLM. The evaluation orchestrator waits at most 2400 seconds (`ENDPOINT_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/serving_config.py`) for the endpoint to come up, and that budget has to cover both the download and vLLM startup. For large checkpoints the download alone takes longer than the budget, so the orchestrator times out and terminates the serving job. Two problems follow: the GPUs sit idle for the whole download, and the timeout kills the download partway through.

Observed with GLM-5.2 (`cyankiwi/GLM-5.2-AWQ-INT4`, 474 GB in 83 weight shards). Job `/karan/eval-20260916-190154-glm-5.2-awq-int4-pp2-1m-3ac6` started mirroring at 19:04 UTC on 2026-09-16 at roughly 106 MB/s and timed out at 19:42 UTC with about 295 GB uploaded. Sixteen H100s were reserved for the full 38 minutes and did no inference. A retry on 2026-09-17 hit the same deadline, so the weights were finally mirrored by a hand-submitted CPU-only job, which took about 70 minutes. Incident record: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/468.

How the jobs fit together today. The eval CLI submits one CPU orchestrator job (`run_evaluation_batch` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py`). The orchestrator submits a GPU child job for inference (`_start_direct_inference` in `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py`). Inside that GPU job, `resolve_model_path` mirrors the Hugging Face repo into the region bucket under a lock and writes a completion marker, and only then does vLLM start. Iris has no job dependency primitive, so ordering between jobs is done by the orchestrator waiting on children.

Proposal: prepare the weights in a separate CPU job before the GPU job is submitted.

- Before submitting the inference job, the orchestrator checks whether the pinned checkpoint already has a completion marker in the region cache.
- On a miss, it submits a small CPU child job (for example `prepare-<run_id>`) that calls the existing mirror function, and waits for it with its own timeout sized for the download rather than for vLLM startup. The job needs enough disk for one shard at a time (about 30 GB for GLM-5.2) and the same region constraint as the GPU job, so the mirror stays in-region.
- The GPU job is submitted only after the prepare job succeeds. Its own `resolve_model_path` call then finds the marker and returns immediately, so nothing in the serving path changes.
- The 2400-second readiness deadline then covers only vLLM startup, which is what it was sized for.

Expected: launching an evaluation against a large uncached checkpoint reserves GPUs only once the weights are in the region cache, and a slow download fails the cheap prepare job instead of the GPU job.

Related: #9230 covers reusing shards that were already uploaded before a mirror was interrupted. That makes an interrupted prepare job resumable, and is independent of this change. #8215 is the pipeline-parallel serving work that first hit this on GLM-5.2. Setting `HF_TOKEN` on the prepare job may raise the download rate, since the current mirror runs unauthenticated and Hugging Face rate-limits anonymous requests.

Done when: an evaluation launch against an uncached large checkpoint runs a CPU prepare job first, the GPU inference job starts with a cache hit, and a test with a fake Iris client covers the miss, hit, and prepare-failure paths.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **How much time serving jobs spend mirroring model weights today (Finelog, last 60 days, partial sample).**

Method. I pulled the `levanter.model_cache` log lines from eval serving workers (`inference-worker-*` tasks) through the Finelog hub. A cold start is a task that logged `model cache miss; populating <path>`; its mirror time is the gap to the `Released lock` line for the same model. Tasks that logged `model cache populated by another worker` sat idle for about the same time. The query server drops many 12-hour windows at its 10-second budget, so this sample covers about 42% of the 60 days. Nothing is scaled below unless marked.

**Cold starts by cluster (sampled windows only)**

| cluster | eval jobs with a cold mirror | with measured time | median | p90 | max | total mirror time | idle accelerator-hours | at list price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cw-rno2a (H100) | 232 | 177 | 7.4 min | 25.7 min | 90.3 min | 31.1 h | 120 | $741 |
| cw-us-east-02a (H100) | 32 | 26 | 7.8 min | 20.4 min | 39.1 min | 4.8 h | 54 | $335 |
| gcp (TPU v5e) | 1 | 1 | 3.6 min | | | 0.1 h | 0.2 | $0 |
| all | 265 | 204 | | | | 36.0 h | 175 | $1,076 |

Warm starts in the same sample: 2,824 tasks hit the cache. So most serving tasks are warm, and the cost sits in the roughly one in ten jobs that bring a new checkpoint.

Idle accelerator-hours = mirror time x accelerators held by the job's serving replicas (tensor x pipeline x data parallel from the vLLM engine config line; 126 of the cold tasks held 8 H100s). For 67 of 265 jobs I could not read the parallel sizes and used the median of other jobs serving the same model. Price is CoreWeave's public on-demand H100 rate, $49.24 per 8-GPU node-hour ($6.16/GPU-hour); the contract rate is lower.

Scaled to the full 60 days by sample coverage: about 410 idle accelerator-hours, about $2,500 at list price, or about $1,300 per month. This excludes the failed runs that motivated this issue, where a mirror outran the 40-minute readiness budget and the job was killed and retried.

**Largest single cold starts**

| model | cluster | mirror time | GPUs idle | idle GPU-hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 | cw-us-east-02a | 37.7 min | 24 | 15.1 |
| MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 | cw-us-east-02a | 39.1 min | 16 | 10.4 |
| MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 | cw-rno2a | 37.8 min | 8 | 5.0 |
| open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02 | cw-rno2a | 36.2 min | 8 | 4.8 |
| nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-BF16 | cw-us-east-02a | 34.1 min | 8 | 4.5 |
| open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8 | cw-rno2a | 32.1 min | 8 | 4.3 |
| open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21 | cw-rno2a | 30.9 min | 8 | 4.1 |

The 67B-A2B family takes 25 to 37 minutes per cold start on cw-rno2a, which matches the 106 MB/s single-stream rate from the GLM-5.2 incident. The same mirrors would run on a CPU node with PR #10277.

**Levanter training.** No `hf-models` cache misses appeared in the sampled windows. The training jobs I found initialize from scratch or from Marin checkpoints, so the CPU prepare step matters less for training right now.

**SkyRL.** SkyRL does not use `levanter.model_cache`. It has its own Hub mirror (`vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/hf_model_cache.py`) that runs on the GPU node before Ray starts, so a cold Hub model also idles the RL gang. vLLM's own timers do not show this: `Loading weights took` excludes the download, and `Model loading took` only includes it when vLLM reads straight from the Hub. In 47 SkyRL tasks the vLLM `Model loading took` time was median 4 s and max 124 s, because the weights were already staged locally or streamed from the regional bucket. I am pulling the `[task-runtime]` staging lines to measure the SkyRL mirror itself and will add that here.

I will update these numbers once the remaining Finelog windows are retried.

- **Levanter HF init** is rare. Only two cache markers exist in the 30-day bucket TTL, both `microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b`. The one I traced is not a training run. It is a Zephyr embedding pipeline that loads the model through `levanter.model_loading`. Its 1.19 GB mirror took 27 s at 194 MB/s.
- **SkyRL** has its own mirror code, not `levanter.model_cache`. All 258 RL tasks are now scanned, apart from 6 whose Finelog queries timed out. Two jobs staged a model cold. One staged on 9 nodes in 1.5 min or less. The other is `benfeuer/opd-identity/mixed/plumbing` on 2026-10-22. Each of its 7 nodes (8 H100s each) downloaded two Hub models before Ray started: `open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1.1` took 44 min and `v0.1` took 7 min. That is about 51 min with 56 GPUs reserved, roughly 48 GPU-hours or $295 at the public H100 price, for one launch.

Serving and Levanter HF init call the same `resolve_cached_model_path`. One Finelog row emitted there would cover both paths. SkyRL would need its own row.

The remaining 12% of windows still time out at the current 10-second Finelog query deadline.

spillover_issues.author: muchanem
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 Filed from the forge full-S run on cw-rno2a, 2026-11-08/09.

## What happens

When a forge driver closes a shellbox sandbox, it calls Iris to kill the child job (`/muchanem/<driver>/shellbox-<id>`). The hub then lists the child job as `killed`, but the pod on cw-rno2a keeps Running, often for hours. Measured 2026-11-08 16:25Z: 1,692 Running sandbox pods for 384 live child jobs; after joining hub child-job states to pod labels, 1,059 pods belonged to jobs already `killed`. Under steady load the leak runs at roughly 50 orphaned pods per minute at ~550 concurrent sandboxes.

Example: `/muchanem/forge-full-s-20261108c-12/shellbox-ea437d76ebe8457192ac6336174c85c5` was `killed` at ~13:08Z and its pod was still Running at 16:25Z.

## Consequences

1. Controller load: the orphans are polled and reconciled like live pods, and exec latency on the controller roughly doubled until they were deleted (RunCommand p50 11.9 s with orphans vs 3.3–4.6 s after cleanup at the same slot count).
2. Node loss: since 19:16Z on 2026-11-08, four nodes (ge6b2c0, g1cc3e2, g1cc352, g86299e) have gone sick with `FailedCreatePodSandBox ... failed to set network "cni-loopback" cached result: write /var/lib/cni/results/...: no space left on device`, and `kubectl exec` into any pod on them returns `Internal error occurred: ... failed to exec in container`. Eight earlier nodes showed the same exec symptom. The kubelet reports no DiskPressure (ephemeral-storage is a different, large volume), so the full filesystem is the node root / CNI state partition that pod sandboxes write to and that un-torn-down pods never release. Twelve of 61 nodes are cordoned as of 02:00Z 2026-11-09.

## Stopgap in place

An external reaper every ~90 s joins `iris job list --prefix /muchanem/<driver>/` states to pod `iris.job_id` labels (the label truncates the shellbox id to 20 hex chars; match by prefix) and deletes pods whose job is terminal. Sick nodes are cordoned and rebooted through the CoreWeave `PhaseState=production-powerreset` status condition.

## Proposed fix (Iris)

- After `TerminateJob`, the controller must verify pod deletion and retry it (the kill RPC returns `Empty`, so the client cannot know). A reconcile pass that deletes any Running pod whose task is terminal would also catch pods leaked by controller restarts.
- Expose the kill outcome (or at least the pod phase) so the client can log it; forge now logs `kill_result=acknowledged returned_state=not_provided` at close because nothing better is available (marin-forge-integration 83dd91dbb2).
- Independently of the leak, exec responses carrying the Kubernetes API error text (`Internal error occurred: ...`) in place of the exit marker should be surfaced as a typed machine-unavailable error, not parsed as an int.

Incident record and evidence excerpts are in Echo: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/952 (incident, response procedure) and https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/953 (ops-log excerpts, node and pod ids, reboot procedure).

`TerminateJob` commits cancellation and returns `Empty`; Kubernetes pod deletion is asynchronous. Current `main` already scans managed active pods every five seconds and deletes attempts absent from the desired task set, so a killed job with a Running pod needs a task-state/desired-set check before adding another reaper. [#10118](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10118) identifies a reconcile/commit race that can restore a cancelled task to RUNNING; it is still open, conflicting, and may explain these pods, but the issue does not include the regional task rows needed to confirm that. The malformed exec exit-code path was fixed by merged [#11076](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11076). [#11079](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11079) separately addresses CoreWeave root-filesystem runtime logs; the CNI write error alone does not identify what filled each node's root filesystem.

Relevant code:
- [`jobs.py#L1102-L1140`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e8eeba00da7aefd98b31620ad8d938e1d442d52d/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/jobs.py#L1102-L1140): cancellation transaction and acknowledgement.

- [`controller.py#L1080-L1103`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e8eeba00da7aefd98b31620ad8d938e1d442d52d/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L1080-L1103): reconcile effects computed before the write transaction.

## Proposed Fix

1. Before the external reaper removes the next sample, capture each child's state and attempt UID from the regional Iris controller alongside the pod's `iris.task_hash`, `iris.attempt_id`, UID, phase, `deletionTimestamp`, and finalizers. Match by task hash and attempt, since `iris.job_id` is truncated. Compare those rows with controller scan/delete logs.
2. If a killed job still has an active task row, rebase and validate the cancellation race fix in #10118 on current `main` instead of opening a parallel PR. Add or retain a deterministic regression for cancellation between reconcile observation and commit, then verify on cw-rno2a at a fixed sandbox count that cancelled children leave the desired set and their pods disappear.
3. If the task is terminal but its pod remains, fix the observed failure in the existing scan/delete path. Test a failed DELETE, a pod surviving an acknowledged DELETE, and a controller restart; keep retrying until a later list confirms absence, and record failures without stopping the rest of the scan. Check `deletionTimestamp` and finalizers before attributing a stuck pod to Iris.
4. Once cleanup converges, expose pending versus completed pod cleanup through a status query so forge can log the physical outcome. Keep `TerminateJob`'s immediate acknowledgement distinct from pod disappearance. Track node root usage and the runtime-log work in #11079 independently of this pod-lifecycle regression.

spillover_issues.title: iris: sandbox pods outlive their killed jobs on cw-rno2a; the leak fills node disks and takes nodes out

spillover_issues.author: muchanem
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

On `cw-rno2a` the Iris controller creates every waiting task pod in one burst per control tick, and at ~1,250 managed sandbox pods the tick takes 3-4 minutes. A task submitted just after a tick starts waits for the whole tick before its pod exists. Measured 2026-11-09 05:12Z with 72 forge drivers (576 slots, ~55 sandbox submissions/min): submit-to-pod-creation p50 118 s, p90 264 s, max 335 s. During 04:10-04:40Z the tail crossed 600 s and forge held ~100 workpieces/hour with `TimeoutError: Iris sandbox did not start within 600 seconds`.

Pods start normally once created (created-to-container-running p50 5 s, max 19 s, n=908), no pods sit Pending in Kubernetes, the controller has `requests.cpu=16` with no limit and no cgroup throttling, and `Control tick failed` is 0. The latency is entirely inside the control tick.

## Evidence

Sandbox pod `creationTimestamp` per 10-second slot, 05:03-05:11Z (every slot not listed had zero creations):

```
05:03:10=174   05:07:20=98 05:07:30=119   05:10:40=159 05:10:50=38
```

Earlier bursts (per 30 s): 04:40:30=66, 04:47:30=75, 04:48:30=90, 04:53:00=44, 04:57:30=21.

Hub view of unstarted sandbox tasks at 05:14Z (hub sync adds ~2 min to the ages): 412 PENDING, 168 of them 5-10 min old; 99 BUILDING 5-10 min old.

Full record with the measurement method: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/954

## Where the time goes

`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py`: one backend tick lists all managed pods, deletes strays, polls every running entry (`_poll_pods`, including finalization `exec`s into finished pods), then applies each `tasks_to_run` entry sequentially, each costing about five Kubernetes API calls (ConfigMap, Pod, get Pod, NetworkPolicy, Secret). Tick length therefore grows with tasks dispatched and finished per tick, and dispatch latency is uniform over the tick length. At a submission rate near one task per second the loop is close to its saturation point, which is why the bursts grew from 20-90 pods to 170-220 pods within half an hour.

## Suggested fixes

- Dispatch outside the reconcile tick, or at least concurrently (a bounded thread pool for the per-task apply calls), so new tasks do not wait for the pod poll of every running task.
- Batch or drop per-task resources where possible (one NetworkPolicy/Secret per job instead of per task; skip the `get Pod` round-trip after `apply`).
- Expose tick duration and dispatch wait as metrics; the controller log rotates in ~20 s at this load, so nothing about tick timing survives.

Related: #11091 (orphan sandbox pods on the same controller; both come from the tick doing too much serially).

Workaround applied on the client side: forge raised its sandbox scheduling timeout from 600 s to 1800 s on `mark/forge-integration`.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`_control_tick` drains pending attempts and calls Kubernetes reconciliation synchronously. `K8sTaskProvider.sync` applies each attempt serially before the cluster scan, so a submission arriving mid-tick waits for the remaining applies, scan, poll, and commit. The `ASSIGNED` redrive path makes pod creation recoverable after a crash, but moving apply off the tick must also change how polling treats a temporarily absent pod. #10118 remains open and touches the same controller and Kubernetes service paths.

**Relevant code**
- [`controller.py#L986-L1100`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e8eeba00da7aefd98b31620ad8d938e1d442d52d/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L986-L1100) — single control tick and blocking reconcile.
- [`dispatch.py#L267-L378`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e8eeba00da7aefd98b31620ad8d938e1d442d52d/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/dispatch.py#L267-L378) — promotion, redrive, and active-task snapshot.
- [`tasks.py#L2577-L2668`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e8eeba00da7aefd98b31620ad8d938e1d442d52d/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2577-L2668) — serial apply followed by cluster scan.
- [`tasks.py#L2817-L2925`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e8eeba00da7aefd98b31620ad8d938e1d442d52d/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2817-L2925) — per-attempt resource ordering and owner UID lookup.

# Kubernetes dispatch latency plan

## Challenges

A pod's Secret and NetworkPolicy are tied to that pod's UID, so removing the post-create Pod GET or sharing those resources across jobs changes ownership and isolation. Polling currently fails an unresolved attempt after a fixed number of scans; an asynchronous apply could still be in flight at that point. Concurrent API calls may also hit CoreWeave rate limits or shared-client thread-safety limits.

## Costs / risks

A dispatcher adds a bounded queue and another lifecycle to shut down cleanly. Extra API concurrency could increase 429s and make all Kubernetes operations slower. #10118 and #10822 touch nearby paths and need to be reconciled before implementation.

## Design

1. Record durable Finelog timing for control-tick phases, time from submission to `ASSIGNED`, time from `ASSIGNED` to Pod creation, per-attempt apply duration, and queue depth. Compare these with the 05:12Z baseline in the [incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/954); the current slow-call logs rotate too quickly to establish a sustained distribution.
2. First try a bounded `ThreadPoolExecutor` for independent attempt applies inside `sync`. Keep ConfigMap/PDB → Pod → NetworkPolicy → Secret order within each attempt, collect results on the control thread, and keep the scan after all applies. Verify the Kubernetes client under concurrent use and cap workers from measured API latency/error rates. This preserves current retry and absent-pod behavior while shortening large apply batches.
3. If the matched-load p90 remains above 60 seconds, move pod application to a bounded dispatcher separate from the control tick. Limit PENDING promotions to available dispatcher capacity, deduplicate queued work by attempt UID, and recover unfinished `ASSIGNED` rows on restart. Return apply failures to the control thread as attempt updates. Keep `ASSIGNED` attempts in flight out of the missing-pod failure path. Check the current attempt before applying; the periodic desired-set scan cleans up a cancellation that races the final create.

## Testing and rollout

Test mixed success and Kubernetes errors, pod creation delayed beyond three scans, cancellation during apply, duplicate redrive, and controller restart with `ASSIGNED` attempts. On cw-rno2a, replay the reported 72-driver, roughly 55-submissions/minute load at about 1,250 managed pods. Compare submit-to-Pod p50/p90/max, tick duration, API 429/error rate, and orphan count against the reported baseline. Target p90 below 60 seconds with no 600-second sandbox start timeouts and no increase in orphaned pods; stop increasing concurrency if API errors rise.

## Open questions

- Which share of the current 3–4 minute tick is spent in apply, cluster scans, polling, and the controller DB?
- Does the shared Kubernetes DynamicClient behave correctly under bounded concurrent applies at this load?

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
**Agent-driven issue** — filed by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

262,144 is the stated context target for the Grug hero shape (#8141) and for extending the 67B-A2B after its 10T run, but no open issue tracks what stands in the way. The epics that used to hold this picture are all closed (#2062, #6047, #1370, #4276, #6656), none of the 14 gates in #8233 mentions sequence length, and #8141 covers attention-kernel qualification only.

The longest sequence trained anywhere so far is 65,536, on TPU v4-2048: two completed cooldowns (#6811, 211B tokens, Paloma macro 2.2772; #6044, 211.3B tokens, 2.224) and a third 1T-token leg running now. On GB200, 65k has run only as short `mhep-ctxext-*` ladder jobs that reached between 100 and 500 of 800 scheduled steps before crashing (#7956). Nothing above 65,536 has trained on any platform.

Blockers, ordered by what gates what.

**Context parallelism is unqualified.** #8141 targets a `data=16, context=4` mesh on 64 GB200s, holding tokens per rank at 65,536. The blocker is the GPU image. TE 2.17.1 fails cuDNN backward graph construction with `CUDNN_STATUS_BAD_PARAM` at `fused_attn_f16_arbitrary_seqlen.cu:934`, reproducing on NVIDIA's own CP4 Ring control at B2/S65536, and the newer TE cannot source-build because `$CUDA_HOME/nvvm/bin/cicc` is absent. `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py` already solves that nvvm layout problem for the vLLM/FlashInfer toolchain. No 64-GPU run has been submitted, and the branch has been idle since 2026-08-11.

**Grug cannot express a sharded sequence axis.** `_GRUG_MESH_AXIS_NAMES` in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/sharding.py` is `("replica_dcn", "data", "expert", "model")`, with no context slot, and `_assert_sequence_axis_unsharded` in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py` rejects sharded q/k/v. Haliax has `ResourceAxis.CONTEXT` with a parity test (#2187, #2188), but that path shards Q and replicates KV on splash attention only, so it does not relieve per-device KV at 262k.

**MoE drop rate at few documents per shard is unmeasured.** Drop rate is governed by cell size and documents per shard, because tokens within a document route coherently and the effective sample size is the document count rather than the token count (#8046). The hero runs 16 documents per shard. At 262k with the token budget held fixed the batch is 16 sequences per rack, so EP64 would see 0.25. #6170 measured overflow fraction roughly doubling per 4x sequence length at EP2, with tokens per step held constant. #8062 specified the arm that would settle this at hero scale, EP64 at 65k seqlen and batch 64, and those jobs are the ones that crashed in #7956 without reporting a drop rate or loss.

**Nothing evaluates past 32k.** The `long_context_32k` bundle caps there, and PG19 is the only slice where sequence length still matters at that point. RULER has not landed in a suite (#7638), and `experiments/evals/long_context_ppl.py` was deleted in #6633. Every 65k result to date is Paloma macro loss against a target preregistered at seqlen 8192, which shows the transition is stable without showing that the model uses the added context.

**Memory headroom is about 1 GiB.** The hero peaks at 137.21 GiB against a 138.22 GiB allocator cap and runs only because that keeps `HloRematerialization` off (#8054). All 48 layers share one `jax.scan` and therefore one remat policy, so global and local layers cannot carry different policies.

Two costing notes for anyone picking this up. #8141 is scoped against the FSDP hero's 512/every-6 attention, while the EP hero moved to 2048/every-4 (#8132, #8227), giving 12 global layers instead of 8. Any 64-device one-shot symmetric collective needs the patched PJRT wheel from #8077, since stock XLA caps `kMaxPeers` at 32.

Done when:

- [ ] #8141 passes its four-GPU CP4 forward/backward gate and reports compile time, steady-state time, peak HBM, and gradient parity at B16/S262144.
- [ ] The #8062 context-extension arm reruns and posts a drop rate and loss at 65k with fewer sequences per batch.
- [ ] A long-context capability eval (RULER or needle-style retrieval) runs on an existing 65k checkpoint.
- [ ] Grug has a context mesh axis with parameters and optimizer state sharded over composite `(data, context)`.
- [ ] EP is shown to compose with CP at long context, or the 262k path records a decision to run FSDP-only. #6656 found degenerate expert routing with EP>1 and CP>1 at 131k in the RL stack.

spillover_issues.title: [grug] Track blockers to 262k-sequence training on GB200

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Grug needs sequence/context parallelism to train the FSDP hero shape at sequence length 262,144. The target layout is `data=16, context=4` on 64 GB200s, with each CP4 group contained within one four-GPU task. NVIDIA Transformer Engine JAX is the strongest existing GPU kernel: it supports Ring and AllGather CP, BF16, GQA, packed THD sequences, causal load balancing, sliding windows, and backward. The current Marin GPU image cannot qualify it. TE 2.17.1 fails during cuDNN backward graph construction on both the exact Grug shapes and NVIDIA's official control, while the newer TE source cannot build because the staged CUDA toolkit lacks `cicc`. No 64-GPU run has been submitted.

## Description

The 262K FSDP hero attention shape is global batch 16, QH48, head dimension 128, and BF16. Forty of 48 layers use KVH12 with SWA512 and half-RoPE. Every sixth layer is global attention with logical KVH6, full causal attention, and NoPE. The current implementation expands global KVH6 back to physical KVH12 before FA4.

CP4 gives 65,536 tokens per rank. The proposed 64-GPU mesh is `(replica=1, data=16, expert=1, model=1, context=4)`, with `context` innermost so CP communication stays within each four-GPU Iris task. Parameters and optimizer state must remain sharded over the composite `(data, context)` axes to preserve the current 64-way FSDP footprint. Batch tensors use `data`; flattened token tensors use `(data, context)`.

The current Grug FA4 wrapper [rejects sequence sharding](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L208-L224), and its backend requires equal Q/K/V sequence lengths. An all-gather-KV baseline therefore still needs rectangular local-Q/full-KV support and global query offsets. A custom ring path would additionally need distributed FP32 log-sum-exp merging and a matching custom VJP.

Transformer Engine's [JAX CP example](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/blob/598b9eacbe9fc34ec105cf8c12f303108ca434ca/docs/examples/jax/attention_context_parallel.py) is the closest reusable GPU implementation. MaxText's [Tokamax ring attention](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/4537) is validated at sequence length 262,144 on TPU and is useful design prior art, but it does not provide a GPU Grug kernel or local SWA.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Qualify an existing distributed attention kernel before extending Grug FA4. Transformer Engine is acceptable if it passes forward and backward for packed THD inputs, gradients match an unsharded reference at short sequence lengths, and the exact local and global 262K shapes fit and improve throughput after communication.

If TE remains unusable, implement global attention as a ring over remote KV blocks and implement local SWA512 with a bounded 511-token left halo. Hidden states should remain in contiguous sequence shards; causal striping should be confined to Q/K/V and packed metadata at the attention boundary.

The experiment is complete when:

1. A CP4 forward/backward control passes on four GB200s with packed segments and rematerialization.
2. The exact B16/S262144 local KVH12/SWA512 and global KVH6/causal cases report compile time, steady-state time, peak HBM, communication, and gradient parity.
3. The 64-GPU `data=16, context=4` run passes with 64-way parameter sharding.
4. Grug handles context-sharded packed metadata, absolute RoPE positions, four causal SConv sites with three-token halos, loss reductions, and MoE routing reductions.

## Status

The [WIP branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention) adds an exact-shape benchmark, a distributed Iris launcher, and the research logbook.

TE 2.17.1 was built and imported on the Marin image after staging CUDA 13 headers, cuDNN frontend, and a task-local NCCL linker path. The exact CP4 Ring cases then failed before XLA compilation or HBM allocation:

```text
fused_attn_f16_arbitrary_seqlen.cu:934
CUDNN_ATTR_OPERATION_RESHAPE_MODE
CUDNN_STATUS_BAD_PARAM
```

The failing Grug jobs were:

- `/dlwh/grug-cp-te217-s262k-ring5-coord/grug-train-grug-cp-te217-s262k-ring5`
- `/dlwh/grug-cp-te217-s262k-ring6-coord/grug-train-grug-cp-te217-s262k-ring6`

Setting `CUDNN_FRONTEND_CUDART_LIB_NAME=libcudart.so.13` removed an incorrect CUDA 12 runtime selection warning but did not change the failure.

NVIDIA's source-pinned CP4 Ring control at B2/S65536/QH128/KVH8/D128/SWA8192 with four packed segments reproduced the same error in `get_fused_attn_bwd_workspace_sizes`. Job: `/dlwh/grug-cp-te217-official-ring-control2-20260810-1535`.

The exact newer TE commit could not be source-built in the current Iris environment. Final job `/dlwh/grug-cp-te-source598-import4-20260810-1544` reached nvcc 13.2.78, then failed CUDA compiler identification because `/app/.venv/nvvm/bin/cicc` was absent. No TE source object or Python extension was built. All GPU allocations were released. AllGather and the 64-GPU gang remain untested.

## Links

* Logbook: [Grug context-parallel attention](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention/.agents/logbooks/grug-context-parallel-attention.md)
* WIP branch: [`codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/compare/main...codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention)
* Benchmark: [`bench_grug_context_parallel_attention.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention/lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_context_parallel_attention.py)
* Launcher: [`context_parallel_attention_benchmark.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention/experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/context_parallel_attention_benchmark.py)
* Prior MarinSkyRL 131K CP campaign: #6656

## Decision Log

- Use CP4 within each four-GPU task and keep FSDP over the composite `data * context = 64` axis.
- Preserve logical KVH6 in global layers instead of expanding it to KVH12 before distributed attention.
- Keep contiguous sequence shards outside attention. TE causal striping would break SConv, RoPE, next-token labels, loss, and packed-segment ordering if carried through the block.
- Do not launch the 64-GPU gang until the four-GPU forward/backward gate passes.
- Do not retry TE 2.17.1 on the current cuDNN 9.19 image. A newer TE attempt requires an image with a complete CUDA development toolkit.

## Conclusion

The exact 262K shape is not yet qualified. TE remains the preferred reuse candidate after a GPU image/toolchain fix because NVIDIA's API covers the required feature set. If the newer TE commit fails its official control on a complete toolchain, proceed with a Grug global ring plus a bounded local-attention halo rather than a generic Ring implementation for all 48 layers.

🤖 **Scope:** Research experiment (64×GB200 run + GPU-image toolchain work), not a <100-line self-contained bug fix — analysis only, no PR. No duplicate PR is open; WIP lives on `codex/research/grug-context-parallel-attention`.

# Research

The two blockers in the Status section have different root causes, and only one is a Marin-side defect.

**Blocker A — TE 2.17.1 cuDNN backward (`CUDNN_STATUS_BAD_PARAM` at `CUDNN_ATTR_OPERATION_RESHAPE_MODE`).** This reproduces on NVIDIA's *own* source-pinned CP4 Ring control (`B2/S65536/QH128/KVH8/D128/SWA8192`, 4 packed segments) in `get_fused_attn_bwd_workspace_sizes`, independent of the Grug shapes. That makes it a TE-2.17.1 / cuDNN-9.19 THD-CP backward defect, not a shape or Marin-integration problem. No Grug-side change fixes it; 2.17.1 is dead on this image, matching the Decision Log. The path forward needs a TE build whose packed-THD CP backward is fixed against the image's cuDNN — i.e. Blocker B must be solved first to even test a newer TE.

**Blocker B — newer TE source build fails: `/app/.venv/nvvm/bin/cicc` absent.** This is a `CUDA_HOME`/nvvm-layout bug, not a missing toolkit. `nvcc` resolves `cicc` at `$CUDA_HOME/nvvm/bin/cicc`; the build set `CUDA_HOME=/app/.venv`, but the nvvm component ships inside the `nvidia-nvvm` pip wheel at `.../site-packages/nvidia/cu13/nvvm/bin/cicc`. Marin already solves exactly this for the vLLM/FlashInfer JIT toolchain — install the nvvm wheel and point `CUDA_HOME` at the wheel dir (`nvcc.parent.parent`), which puts `cicc` on the expected `$CUDA_HOME/nvvm/bin` path. Reuse that bootstrap for the TE build instead of a bespoke `CUDA_HOME`.

**Relevant code**
- [`vllm_server.py#L54-L82`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py#L54-L82) — nvcc+crt+**nvvm** wheels; `CUDA_HOME` set to wheel dir so `cicc` resolves
- [`_fa4_cute.py#L208-L217`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L208-L217) — rejects sequence-axis sharding (the code-side blocker for any Grug-native CP fallback)

# Proposed approach (for human review before implementation)

1. **Fix the TE toolchain (highest leverage, small).** Give the TE source build the same CUDA toolchain bootstrap as vLLM: add `nvidia-nvvm` (matching the nvcc/crt CUDA-13 pins) and set `CUDA_HOME` to the nvcc wheel's `parent.parent` so `$CUDA_HOME/nvvm/bin/cicc` exists. This unblocks building any newer TE, a prerequisite for retesting Blocker A. It lives on the research branch, not `main`.
2. **Qualify newer TE against its own control first.** Run NVIDIA's `B2/S65536/QH128/KVH8` CP4 Ring forward+backward control before touching Grug shapes. If it still throws the reshape-mode error on cuDNN 9.19, the image needs a newer cuDNN and TE is not viable on the current image regardless of version.
3. **Only then** run the four-GPU CP4 forward/backward gate on the exact Grug local-KVH12/SWA512 and global-KVH6/causal cases, per the Decision Log's "no 64-GPU gang until the four-GPU gate passes."
4. **Fallback (if newer TE fails its control on a complete toolchain):** Grug global ring over remote KV blocks + bounded 511-token left-halo local SWA, keeping contiguous sequence shards outside attention. This requires lifting the `_assert_sequence_axis_unsharded` guard for the ring path and adding rectangular local-Q/full-KV support + a custom VJP with distributed FP32 log-sum-exp merging.

spillover_issues.author: WhenWen
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Evaluate whether factorizing every Grug MoE linear projection as `v * (Wx)`, with fixed row norms for baseline MuonH matrices and fixed L2 norms for `v`, improves effective training speed over the July MoE baseline. The implementation is validated and both Gate-1 cells are running normally.

## Description

The experiment keeps every baseline matrix initialization unchanged and initializes every output scale vector `v` to one, so the effective network is identical at step 0. Grug stores matrices as `(input, output)`, so mathematical row norms reduce over the stored input axis. The LM-head matrix remains on AdamH; router and attention-gate matrices retain their baseline Adam path; all `v` parameters use AdamH.

Gate 1 compares two v5p-8 cells:

- `MOE-ROW-NORM-001`: d512, batch 16, 10,980 steps, 3.82e17 FLOPs; baseline macro loss 3.5667 and 352,609 tokens/s.
- `MOE-ROW-NORM-002`: d768, batch 32, 16,875 steps, 2.81e18 FLOPs; baseline macro loss 3.2272 and 249,954 tokens/s.

Initiating prompt:

> Can you try on our moe baseline a mild improvement
>
> Write every linear as f(x; v, W) = v * (Wx) and fix row norm of W and L2 norm of v
>
> Initialize v to be all 1 at beginning and W to be the same as now
>
> Use AdamH on v and MuonH on W (but variant of MuonH where the normalization is per row)
>
> Note that here the row and column may or may not be the same as convention of the original jax framing so be careful about this
>
> For the matrix where originally we use AdamH, keep using AdamH (like LM head)

## Hypothesis or Goal

Separating per-output scale from direction will improve loss enough to offset any throughput cost, yielding effective speedup greater than 1 at both Gate-1 widths.

## Status

Both requested v5p-8 children are running under Iris parent `/kaiyuew/moe-row-norm-gate1-8131`. Their W&B identities/configs, finite losses, advancing timestamps, and checkpoint roots are verified. Final Paloma loss and effective-speedup decisions are pending terminal metrics.

## Links

- Branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/moe-row-norm-8131
- Logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/moe-row-norm-8131/.agents/logbooks/moe-row-norm-gate1.md
- d512 W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-ROW-NORM-001-d512
- d768 W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-ROW-NORM-002-d768
- Healthy-startup update: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8131#issuecomment-5246287197

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-10: Preserve baseline optimizer exceptions: LM-head `W` remains AdamH; router and zero-initialized attention-gate `W` remain Adam.
- 2026-08-10: Normalize mathematical output rows over stored axis `-2` because Grug weights use `(..., input, output)`.
- 2026-08-10: Pin the CPU StepRunner parent to `us-central1` so its v5p-8 children inherit a schedulable region.

## Conclusion

Pending terminal Gate-1 results.

spillover_issues.author: hammer
spillover_issues.body:
This came out of reviewing the Swiss-AI Apertus-2 MoE pretraining fork (https://github.com/swiss-ai/Megatron-LM-MoE) against Marin's grug MoE code. Marin does not have Apertus's FP8 storage of MoE activations: their memory-efficient MoE keeps expert activations in FP8 to fit GH200/Grace nodes where HBM is scarce relative to host RAM. Marin should not copy the paired weight-offload — FSDP already distributes expert weights across the rack's HBM over NVLink, and parking them on Grace would add C2C to the per-layer critical path — but the FP8-activation half lands directly on a live Marin constraint.

That constraint is #8054: the FSDP hero is HBM-pressure-bound on GB200. The whole +9% MFU win there was 3.69 GiB of peak crossing under the XLA rematerialization limit (138.22 GiB), and both ways to buy headroom OOM'd on the size of the bf16 MoE dispatch tensors — `save_moe` requested 386.7 GiB of device memory (two ~155 GB dispatch tags live across all 48 layers) and `offload_moe` needed a 144 GiB pinned-host arena Grace couldn't spare. Those tensors (`_CHECKPOINT_DISPATCH_INPUT` / `_CHECKPOINT_DISPATCH_OUTPUT`, tagged by `MOE_REMAT_SAVE_NAMES` in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/scatter.py`) are bf16. Storing them in FP8 at the remat boundary roughly halves both requests (~193 GiB device / ~72 GiB host), which could flip `save_moe`/`offload_moe` from infeasible to feasible at hero shape — the same memory pressure Apertus's FP8 activations relieve on Grace.

Marin already has the FP8 pieces to do this in JAX — #6911 (FP8 dispatch/combine) and #7282 (MXFP8 grouped MoE GEMM) — so no new kernels are needed, just an FP8 cast around the tagged tensors, and none of Apertus's Megatron/Triton code has to port. This is orthogonal to whether FP8 compute pays off (contested; #7282's throughput win was retracted): here FP8 buys memory-threshold headroom, not FLOPs, so it is judged on peak HBM and feasibility, not on MFU from quantized matmuls. It composes with the #8054 top open item (splitting the 48-layer `jax.scan` for a per-layer remat policy) rather than replacing it.

Done when:
- `save_moe` and/or `offload_moe` can store the tagged MoE dispatch tensors in FP8 instead of bf16, behind a flag, with the fp8 format and scaling named.
- Peak HBM (and pinned-host arena for `offload_moe`) is re-measured at hero shape (d6144, 4-of-128, 64x GB200); the target is one of the two fitting where it OOM'd in #8054.
- A short check confirms FP8 dispatch storage is loss-neutral vs bf16 at gate-1 scale (these are activations, not weights, so tolerance is generous).

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read fix-issue + commit skills, AGENTS.md
- [x] Actionability check — actionable, but large scope (feature + hero HBM re-measurement + loss validation)
- [x] Locate remat plumbing and FP8 primitives; duplicate-work preflight
- [ ] Human review of proposed approach before implementation

Scope call: this needs a 64x GB200 hero-shape HBM re-measurement and a gate-1 loss check, not a self-contained <100-line fix. Per the agent workflow I'm posting root-cause analysis + a proposed approach for review rather than opening a PR. No overlapping PR exists (related: #7282, #6911/#7665).

# Research

`save_moe`/`offload_moe` are `RematMode` literals in the hero FSDP model; they become JAX checkpoint policies over the tensors tagged by `tree_checkpoint_name(...)`. Those tags are bf16, so `save_only_these_names` keeps ~386.7 GiB on device and the offload policy needs a ~144 GiB pinned-host arena — both OOM at hero shape (#8054). Casting the tagged tensor to FP8 *before* the checkpoint-name tag makes the saved/offloaded residual FP8, roughly halving both requests, while the tag's consumers keep working on a dequantized bf16 value. Memory-threshold play, independent of whether FP8 *compute* pays off.

**Relevant code**
- [`moe_hero_fsdp/model.py#L1010-L1020`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eafa4d49f7c55fbf2abb26b5d92c1ac7d093f9fb/experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/model.py#L1010-L1020) — `remat_mode` → `save_only_these_names` / `save_and_offload_only_these_names`
- [`moe_hero_fsdp/model.py#L61-L65`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eafa4d49f7c55fbf2abb26b5d92c1ac7d093f9fb/experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/model.py#L61-L65) — `offload_moe` parks only `_CHECKPOINT_DISPATCH_OUTPUT`
- [`_moe/common.py#L42-L56`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eafa4d49f7c55fbf2abb26b5d92c1ac7d093f9fb/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/common.py#L42-L56) — the four checkpoint tags / `MOE_REMAT_SAVE_NAMES`
- [`_moe/scatter.py#L41-L50`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eafa4d49f7c55fbf2abb26b5d92c1ac7d093f9fb/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/scatter.py#L41-L50) — bf16 `tree_checkpoint_name` on dispatch in/out (mirrored in `ep_ring.py`, `ep_deepep.py`, `sonic*.py`)
- [`haliax/_src/fp8.py#L32-L64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eafa4d49f7c55fbf2abb26b5d92c1ac7d093f9fb/lib/haliax/src/haliax/_src/fp8.py#L32-L64) — `quantize` / `dequantize` / `compute_scale` primitives to reuse

# Proposed Approach

**Mechanism.** A small helper wraps the existing tag: cast to FP8 with a scale, tag the FP8 array, dequantize back to bf16 for downstream ops.

```python
# in _moe/common.py, reused by every backend
def _checkpoint_fp8(x, name, *, enabled, fp8_dtype=jnp.float8_e4m3fn):
    if not enabled:
        return tree_checkpoint_name(x, name)
    scale = _dispatch_scale(x, fp8_dtype)          # per-tensor amax -> scale
    q = tree_checkpoint_name(quantize(x, fp8_dtype, scale, x.dtype), name)
    return dequantize(q, x.dtype, scale)           # recomputed in bwd; cheap
```

`save_only_these_names` saves exactly the checkpoint-named value, so tagging the FP8 array is what makes the saved/offloaded residual FP8; the trailing `dequantize` is recomputed in backward and is negligible.

**Flag.** Thread an `moe_dispatch_fp8: bool` (default `False`) from the hero config down to the backend calls — do **not** overload `remat_mode`, since FP8 storage should compose with both `save_moe` and `offload_moe`. Format `e4m3` (activations, generous range); scaling via per-tensor dynamic amax (`compute_scale`), per-row as a follow-up if needed.

**Which tags.** The two ~155 GB tensors are `_CHECKPOINT_DISPATCH_INPUT` and `_CHECKPOINT_DISPATCH_OUTPUT`. `offload_moe` currently offloads only the output; FP8 there alone drops the ~144 GiB host arena to ~72 GiB. For `save_moe`, FP8 on both dispatch tags is what moves 386.7 GiB toward ~193 GiB. Leave `_CHECKPOINT_EXPERT_HIDDEN` bf16 unless measurement shows otherwise — it feeds the down-proj GEMM directly.

**Open questions for review**
1. Does XLA actually hold the FP8 buffer, or fuse `quantize`→`dequantize` and keep bf16? Needs a compiled-HLO / peak-HBM check before trusting the halving — the whole win rests on this.
2. Static vs dynamic scale for the offloaded output: dynamic amax adds a reduction on the forward hot path; a fixed scale avoids it but risks clipping. Prefer dynamic for the loss gate, revisit for speed.
3. Backends to cover — start with the hero path (`ep_ring`/`ep_deepep`), factor the helper in `common.py` so `scatter`/`sonic*` inherit it.

**Done-when mapping (needs GB200 + gate-1 runs I can't execute here)**
- FP8 storage behind `moe_dispatch_fp8`, `e4m3` + dynamic per-tensor scale — implementable.
- Peak HBM / pinned-host re-measured at d6144, 4-of-128, 64x GB200 — requires the hero cluster.
- Gate-1 loss-neutral FP8-vs-bf16 check — requires a training run.

If a maintainer confirms the mechanism and points at a GB200 slot for the HBM/HLO check, I can land the backend + flag change and wire the measurement. Flagging for review before writing code that can't be validated here.

spillover_issues.author: hammer
spillover_issues.body:
The two-gate isoFLOP promotion decision for grug variants runs on `loss(C) = L∞ + A·C^(-α)` (L∞ and α pinned, only A fit) and an `effective_speedup()` calculation. Neither is code: both live as prose plus a snippet in `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md` and `experiments/grug/moe/README.md`, retyped per ablation and computed offline. The constants have already drifted — `agent.md` carries `A=88.32` where #4447 fit `95.18`. So the number that gates every variant has no test, no logged provenance, and no reported uncertainty. `lib/marin/src/marin/scaling_laws/isoflop_analysis.py` fits a different law (Chinchilla Approach 2, optimal-tokens `D*~A·C^α`, no asymptote), so the envelope and speedup math have no shared home.

Done when:
- `marin.scaling_laws` has a tested module for the `L∞ + A·C^(-α)` envelope and `effective_speedup`, beside `isoflop_analysis.py`. The pinned asymptote is an explicit, eval-tagged parameter (1.6 is paloma-macro-specific; DCLM is ~1.9), not a magic number.
- Tests cover the `agent.md` worked example (A ≈ 87.7) and the budget-invariance identity `speedup == ((L_worse - L∞) / (L_better - L∞)) ** (1/α)`.
- Each speedup reports the 90% lack-of-fit interval (Student-t, n−2 dof for the 4-point fit, see #6757), so a promotion is not gated on a bare point estimate.
- The grug ablation harness calls it and logs `effective_speedup`, fitted `A`, and the gate verdict, feeding #7970 instead of a hand-pasted issue table.
- `agent.md` and `README.md` reference the module instead of the inline snippet.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue, confirm actionable
- [x] Research codebase (scaling_laws module, grug harness, docs)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight
- [x] Post analysis (scope is a new multi-module feature, not a <100-line bug fix — no PR per agent policy)

Actionable and well-scoped, but this is a **new module + tests + harness wiring + doc edits** across `lib/marin` and `experiments/grug/moe`, and one bullet is coupled to #7970. That exceeds the small-self-contained-fix bar, so this is analysis for human sign-off rather than an auto-PR.

# Research

The gate math is prose, not code: the envelope `loss(C) = L∞ + A·C^(-α)` and `effective_speedup()` live only as a snippet + worked example in `agent.md`/`README.md` and are recomputed offline per ablation. `scaling_laws/isoflop_analysis.py` fits a *different* law (Chinchilla Approach 2, `D*≈A·C^α`, no asymptote), so the envelope and speedup math have no shared, tested home and no logged provenance/uncertainty. Constants have already drifted — `agent.md` pins the envelope at `88.32` (May drop-1e18 fit) while the v16 reference curve is `95.18` (#4447) — with no test to catch it.

**Relevant code**
- [`agent.md` L27-L46`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/agent.md#L27-L46) — envelope `1.6 + 88.32·C^(-0.0941)`, gate-1/gate-2 rules
- [`agent.md` L66-L93](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/agent.md#L66-L93) — `effective_speedup()` snippet + `A ≈ 87.7` worked example
- [`README.md` L125-L139](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/README.md#L125-L139) — inline `88.32` vs `95.18` reference curves
- [`isoflop_analysis.py` L275-L367](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/scaling_laws/isoflop_analysis.py#L275-L367) — different law; no asymptote/speedup
- [`scaling_laws/__init__.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/scaling_laws/__init__.py) — public surface to extend

# Proposed approach

New `lib/marin/src/marin/scaling_laws/effective_speedup.py`, exported from `__init__.py`, beside `isoflop_analysis.py`.

**Types + eval-tagged asymptote (not a magic 1.6):**

```python
# Pinned asymptote is eval-specific: paloma-macro ≈ 1.6, DCLM ≈ 1.9.
PINNED_ASYMPTOTE: dict[str, float] = {"paloma_macro": 1.6, "dclm": 1.9}

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PinnedEnvelope:
    """loss(C) = l_inf + A * C**(-alpha); l_inf pinned per eval, A (and alpha) fit."""
    eval_tag: str
    l_inf: float
    alpha: float
    A: float

    def loss(self, flops: float) -> float: ...
    def flops_for_loss(self, loss: float) -> float: ...  # invert
```

**Two entry points, matching the two gates:**

- `effective_speedup(baseline_loss, baseline_tps, variant_loss, variant_tps, budget, *, l_inf, alpha) -> float` — gate-1. α pinned to the baseline exponent, A recentered through the baseline point, invert for `C_needed`, compare wall-clock. This is the current snippet made testable.
- `fit_envelope(points, *, eval_tag, l_inf, fit_alpha=True) -> tuple[PinnedEnvelope, LackOfFit]` — gate-2. Fit `log(loss - l_inf) = log A - α·log C` by least squares over the 4 optima (2 params → **n−2 dof**), project to 1e21/1e23.

**Uncertainty (#6757):** `LackOfFit` reports the 90% Student-t lack-of-fit interval (n−2 dof for the 4-point fit) on the fitted curve, propagated to the projected loss and to `effective_speedup`, so a promotion is never gated on a bare point estimate.

**Meaningful tests (fail when the math is wrong):**
- `agent.md` worked example: `fit A` through the d512 baseline point ⇒ `A ≈ 87.7`.
- Budget-invariance identity: at equal tps, `effective_speedup == ((L_worse - l_inf)/(L_better - l_inf)) ** (1/alpha)` — verifies recentre+invert is compute-scale-free.
- Round-trip: `envelope.flops_for_loss(envelope.loss(C)) == C`.
- Lack-of-fit interval widens as residuals grow and covers the point estimate.

**Docs + harness:**
- Replace the inline snippet/constants in `agent.md` and `README.md` with a reference to the module (kills the 88.32/95.18 drift; constants live in one place).
- Wiring the grug ablation harness to *call* the module and log `effective_speedup`, fitted `A`, and the gate verdict is coupled to #7970 (that issue defines the ablation decision-metadata fields). Today that "harness" is prose in `agent.md`, not code. **Recommend:** land the tested module + doc references first; do the harness/metadata wiring as a follow-up on the #7970 branch so both land against a real schema.

**Suggested split:** (1) tested `effective_speedup.py` + doc references (self-contained, ~1 module + tests); (2) harness/logging wiring under #7970. Requesting a 👍 on this API shape (esp. the `PINNED_ASYMPTOTE` registry and fitting α in gate-2 vs pinning it in gate-1) before implementing part 1.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue tracks grug MoE quantile-balancing ablations that compare the existing chunk-quantile averaging estimator against per-sequence, fixed logit histogram, K3 sigmoid histogram, dynamic histogram, and after-sigmoid variants. The planned d768/d1024/d1280 sweep did not fully run as originally scoped: the estimator comparison that executed on August 7-8, 2026 was d768 only, while separate QB-bias runs covered d768/d1024/d1280. The useful current state is the run map in the August 17 update, including two crashed histogram variants; the issue still needs a final loss/load-balance synthesis before changing the default estimator.

### Helpful links
- [Run map comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8033#issuecomment-5320860256)
- [CHUNK_QUANTILE baseline: qb-abl-normal](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-normal)
- [PER_SEQUENCE: qb-abl-perseq](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-perseq)
- [LOGIT_HIST: qb-abl-logithist](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-logithist)
- [K3_HIST: qb-abl-k3hist](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qb-abl-k3hist)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

grug MoE balances expert load with **QB**: each step it overwrites the per-expert router bias from a target quantile of each expert's routing scores over the batch (top-4 of 128 experts). Two families estimate that quantile:

- **Chunk-quantile / averaging** — exact `(1−k/n)` quantile per chunk, then average. Chunk = per-GPU shard (current `local` default, topology-dependent) or per-sequence (topology-independent). "Histogram vs Avg" refers to this averaging family.
- **Histogram** — accumulate a per-expert histogram, read one quantile. `logit_hist` (fixed logit range) or `k3_hist` (Kimi-K3, sigmoid-score space, adaptive `[bmin−1, bmax+1]` range).

Two known concerns motivate the sweep:
- **Dropping / coverage.** A fixed-range logit histogram silently **drops** out-of-range values (`jnp.histogram` excludes them rather than clamping), truncating the upper tail and biasing the `~0.969` target quantile. Score-space (K3) is bounded to `[0,1]` so it covers by construction; logit-space is unbounded and does not.
- **Histogram vs averaging.** A prior simple histogram was found worse than chunk-quantile (binning + range-calibration error beating the histogram's theoretical unbiasedness); we want to quantify this cleanly and see whether the K3 score-space histogram closes the gap.

## Hypothesis / Goal

Identify the best QB estimator for grug MoE by loss **and** load-balance quality, and settle:
1. **Histogram vs averaging** — reproduce and quantify the gap on matched configs.
2. **Dropping / coverage** — measure token-drop rate and expert-load imbalance per estimator, plus histogram out-of-range coverage (logit min/max, fraction outside range).
3. **Topology-independence** — per-sequence chunk-quantile vs per-device `local`.

Estimators under test (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/model.py`, `qb_estimator`):
- `local` — per-device chunk-quantile (current default)
- per-sequence chunk-quantile (new, topology-independent)
- `logit_hist` — fixed-range logit histogram (+ coverage instrumentation / clamp variant)
- `k3_hist` — adaptive sigmoid-score histogram

## Setup (planned)

- **Ablation sizes:** d768, d1024, d1280 (downsized grug MoE hero shape; architecture/data/eval/optimizer/steps held fixed, vary only `qb_estimator`).
- **Metrics:** paloma macro loss, uncheatable bpb, per-expert load balance (max/mean load, drop rate), and for histograms the out-of-range coverage fraction.

## Status

Runs were launched for the d768 estimator comparison and the three-size QB-bias checks. A final metric synthesis is still needed before making a recommendation.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8033#issuecomment-5320860256

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

Part of #6711

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Histogram balances slightly better than averaging: biases have a mean around zero, with range from -20 ish to 10 ish: Appying bias to before sigmoid gives much better performance. Red bar is Kimi style after sigmoid. Blue bar is histogram before sigmoid, but capping the bins to -8 to 8. This does worse, as the bins need to extend out about twice as far. comments.author: ClassicLarry

(That seems perhaps more plausible to me, compared to the alternative that Kimi and Deepseek are applying it to the less efficient position. Or Kimi didn't test pre-sigmoid and went with the location with simpler histogram bounds?) Regardless, it seems our best near term path forward is to go with the implementation that looks best on our data, which is pre-sigmoid.

spillover_issues.title: Agent MoE Experiment: QB Dropping and Histogram vs Avg

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue asks two separate questions:

1. Can Grug train from initialization when only routed expert weights are shared across layers?
2. Can an already-trained untied Grug checkpoint be converted into that architecture?

The architecture answer is yes across d512, d768, d1024, and d1280. The tied-minus-control Paloma penalties are `+0.038167`, `+0.028548`, `+0.030765`, and `+0.029795`. The d1280 treatment removes 46.154% of routed-expert parameters and passes the raw non-growth, compression-normalized, routing, and update-health gates. None of the tested tied models is an effective-speed win, so this is an existence proof for the Theseus target architecture rather than a better training recipe.

The first conversion campaign shows partial recovery but misses promotion. The best one-pair d512 student finishes +0.027693 validation and +0.025834 Paloma above its untied teacher after 250.09M online tokens; the fixed limits are +0.020 and +0.030. Spectral probes alter 153/256 assignments relative to native matching, improve their own objective by only 0.51%, and worsen immediate model loss. Spectral matching is dropped from the recipe.

The remaining signal is at the whole routed-function level. Per-expert prefit improves one source layer by sacrificing the other. Fixed-route whole-bank prefit fits cached outputs but does not improve rollout recovery. Router unlocking, affected norms, rank-8 layer conditioning, and an untied capacity oracle do not explain the residual gap. `GRUG-XEM-010` removed expert correspondence entirely and jointly fit one shared bank and both routers against complete cached teacher MoE outputs. It failed its offline gate: best held-out normalized MSE was 0.376287 versus the required 0.349847, only 251/256 and 253/256 experts were active, and the train/held-out split showed strong overfitting. No online screen launched.

The large `GRUG-XEM-009` fresh-training comparison was canceled after 3 hours 48 minutes waiting for central2 capacity. Neither arm received a TPU or produced a W&B run or checkpoint. It will not be retried from this registration.

`GRUG-XEM-011` passed the d1024 architecture gate. The tied model finished +0.030765 Paloma above its matched control while removing 45.455% of expert parameters; routing and shared-bank updates were healthy. The raw penalty grew by 0.002217 from d768, and effective speed was 0.812x, so tying remains an architecture target rather than a compute-speed recipe.

`GRUG-XEM-012`, the final registered central1 architecture-scale comparison, is complete. At d1280 the tied model finishes at Paloma `2.929653406` versus control `2.899857998`, delta `+0.029795408`. It passes the `+0.040` architecture, `+0.030764580` raw non-growth, and `+0.031237881` compression-normalized limits. Its final-100 window has exact metric cardinality, zero overflow, all 256 experts active per layer over the window, entropy above 5.3, and balanced tied-bank updates. No further width or post-hoc surgery is authorized by this result.
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Terms used in this issue

Grug is this repository's JAX MoE training recipe. `d512` and `d768` are model widths. Both use 256 routed experts and top-4 routing. A topology tuple maps Transformer layers to expert-bank IDs. For example, `(0,1,2,2,3,4)` means layers 2 and 3 share bank 2; the other layers use distinct banks.

Only the routed experts' gate, up, and down projections are shared. Attention, routers, router QB bias and pending QB state, RMSNorm/GatedNorm, always-on dense MLPs, and residual blocks remain layer-specific. QB is Grug's non-gradient router-balancing mechanism: top-k threshold statistics collected on one update change the next update's router bias.

The work uses six distinct operations:

| Operation | Definition |
|---|---|
| Tied-from-scratch training | Initialize a new model whose configured layers share a single expert-bank pytree leaf. This tests the architecture. |
| Correspondence conversion | Remove one trained source bank, retain layer 2's bank, and permute layer 3's router columns and QB state with a chosen expert bijection. No training occurs. |
| Legacy fixed-route prefit | Train only the shared bank on cached teacher outputs while replaying teacher-selected expert IDs and combine weights. |
| Stage A | Online frozen-router local recovery. Only the shared bank receives gradient updates. The full student generates current layer states, and each untied teacher MoE is evaluated on that student state. The original Stage A used routed-MoE loss only; the later selected arm used routed-MoE `1.0` + CE `0.05` + teacher-logit KL `0.1`. QB updates are frozen. |
| Stage B | Online preservation recovery. The shared bank and affected router matrices receive gradients; ordinary QB updates resume. The objective is CE `1.0` + teacher-logit KL `0.1` + teacher-on-student-state routed-MoE loss `1.0`. Attention, norms, dense MLPs, embeddings/head, and unmerged banks stay frozen. |
| Correspondence-free refactor | The new `GRUG-XEM-010` offline operation. Train one shared bank and both router matrices against complete cached teacher routed outputs. The student generates its own hard top-4 routes. Teacher expert IDs, combine weights, assignments, and matching artifacts are discarded. This is neither Stage A nor Stage B. |

“Online tokens” count only full-model recovery. Offline refactor or prefit optimizer steps never count toward a token deadline.
